items.abstract: I explore the relationship between psychiatric diagnoses, lived experience, and knowledge in participatory research. It has been claimed that people who have a particular psychiatric diagnosis have unique knowledge about that psychiatric diagnosis which everyone else lacks. Advocates have used critical realism to justify basing lived experience research around psychiatric diagnoses. I suggest there is no straightforward way to think that psychiatric diagnoses relate to knowledge through lived experience. Two challenges need addressing. First, when we link psychiatric diagnoses to lived experience we can understand this as relating to categorical understandings or dimensional understandings of the psychiatric diagnosis. Whether the psychiatric diagnosis is taken as categorical or dimensional has a significant impact upon who should be taken as having lived experience. Second, there are potentially alternative diagnoses which have a better connection to lived experience than currently used psychiatric diagnoses do. Alternative diagnoses which are more homogeneous would result in more commonality of lived experience. I outline my own solution by portraying psychiatric diagnoses as idealized and abstract models. Given that no model fully describes reality, we should use a plurality of approaches. For example, when conducting participatory research on people currently diagnosed as autistic, different participatory studies should use categorical notions of autism, dimensional notions of autism, substantive subtypes of autism and alternatives which completely dispense with autism. Finally, how lived experience research could occur in relation to categorical approaches, dimensional approaches, Research Domain Criteria and Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology is outlined.

items.title: Functional Delusional Beliefs and Moral Responsibility.
items.abstract: Delusional beliefs are often associated with mental illness, and it is linked with schizophrenia spectrum and delusional disorder. Delusions are characterized as a failure of reasoning, and patients with delusions typically view their actions as caused by impervious beliefs. For this reason, a person with delusions loses their sense of agency and ownership, which is usually treated as an excusing condition for moral responsibility. We argue that this is not true in all cases. Lisa Bortolotti claims that some delusional beliefs contribute to achieving the patient’s epistemic goals and maintaining their sense of epistemic agency. Following this, we offer an analysis of patients with delusional beliefs to show that in cases where such beliefs remain epistemically functional, a patient could still be morally responsible. Our analysis is twofold: 1) we discuss the basis of moral exemption for a person with delusions owing to mental illness, and then 2) we examine the epistemic value of delusional belief in schizophrenia spectrum cases, its significance in epistemic agency, and what this implies for moral responsibility.

items.title: Lacunar Creativity: A Phenomenological Theory of Creative Genesis.
items.abstract: The emergence of genuinely new ideas remains an open problem in the philosophy of creativity and cognitive science. Existing accounts often oscillate between gradualist models, which reduce novelty to incremental recombination, and intuitive approaches that lack clear structural criteria. This article proposes a theory of creative genesis as a phenomenological process of discontinuity, in which novelty emerges from a lived experience of cognitive saturation, followed by rupture and retroactive reintegration of a conceptual field. Prominent accounts have emphasized creativity as a systemic interaction between individual, domain, and social validation, as in the systems model proposed by Csikszentmihalyi, or as a function of optimal experiential states such as flow. We introduce the concept of lacunar creativity to designate this mode of genesis, characterized by the perception of a meaningful gap and the reconfiguration of the space of possibilities itself. In contrast, recombinative creativity refers to processes that generate novelty through exploration and rearrangement within a stable horizon of intelligibility. We argue that both forms are legitimate yet structurally distinct, and that conflating them has generated recurrent conceptual impasses in creativity research. Based on this framework, we examine implications for artificial intelligence, particularly in light of the recent emergence of large-scale artificial language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. While these systems display unprecedented capacities for generative variation and recombination, we argue that they do not currently satisfy the phenomenological conditions required for lacunar creative genesis. The proposed framework offers non-anthropocentric criteria for evaluating creativity across human and artificial agents, while remaining open to future developments.

items.title: A Brief Historical and Neuropsychoanalytic Overview of Theories on Movement and Psychomotor Function.
items.abstract: This article systematizes theories of psychomotor disorders, human movement and psychomotor function. In it, we summarize the classical neuroanatomical theories of Vesalius, Brodmann, Charcot, and Luria; the fundamental psychoanalytic ideas of the psychic apparatus of Freud and Klein; and the contemporary neuropsychoanalytic concepts of Solms and Turnbull. As a result, we distinguish three main groups of theories: structural (with a neuroanatomical focus), linear (connecting the psychic with the physical aspect), and neuroplastic (looking for similarities between neuronal plasticity and the psychic adaptability of the psychic apparatus). These theories are presented in chronological order, with structural theories preceding linear theories, and linear theories serving as a transition to neuroplastic theories. In conclusion, psychomotor skills and synaptic conduction in the brain depend on the overall integrity of the organism, the interactions of the individual with the environment, and concomitant changes in neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, glutamate, and cortisol.

items.title: Diagnoxia Nervosa: A Critique of the Quest to Validate Orthorexia Nervosa.
items.abstract: Orthorexia nervosa (ON) is a term coined to describe clinical cases of individuals obsessing over quality of food to the point of leading to nutritional deficiencies and related health complications. Some researchers advocate for ON to be medicalized as a formal diagnosis. Research on this topic is disproportionately focused on correlational, individual factors into the etiology of ON while the minority consider sociocultural factors into the development of this trend. I argue that this research trend is questionable, with overly narrow focus on individual symptomatology, a lack of consideration for sociocultural context, and a lack of disprovable hypotheses, leading to hindered clarity and quality of research findings. I argue in favor of clarifying distinctions between the role of researchers searching for a fuller understanding of the matter, the role of clinicians in taking reactive measures aiding orthorexic clients, and the role of preventative health care specialists in taking proactive measures addressing trending orthorexic behaviors exhibited in society.

items.title: From flow to mystical experiences: Connecting entropy and fluency along the unifying framework of cognitive continuum.
items.abstract: Self-transcendent experiences (STEs) represent profound shifts in cognition and consciousness, possessing significant transformative potential. With growing scientific interest in these phenomena, we propose the cognitive continuum as a unifying framework. Grounded in enactive cognitive science and complex dynamic systems perspectives, this approach takes the embodied person, embedded within their world, as the appropriate unit of analysis. The continuum illustrates how STEs, such as flow states and mystical experiences, reflect an enhancement of relevance realization, the organism’s active engagement with its environment to adaptively frame its world, across increasingly global levels of cognitive organization. We identify destabilization and complexification as central processes in this enhancement and propose entropy as their metric. We introduce the Entropy-Fluency hypothesis, which posits that increased entropy signals destabilization followed by increased fluency, thereby conceptually bridging first-person subjective experiences with third-person scientific observations of STEs. The cognitive continuum reveals STEs as dynamic, person-specific, and context-dependent phenomena emerging from person-world coupling, requiring idiographic and transdisciplinary methodological approaches. This framework provides conceptual tools for understanding these profound experiences, contributing to a comprehensive science of human flourishing.

items.title: Spacetime functionalism and the collapse problem.
items.abstract: Recent work in quantum gravity (QG) suggests that spacetime is not fundamental. Rather, spacetime emerges from an underlying non-spatiotemporal reality. Spacetime functionalism has been proposed as one way to make sense of the emergence of spacetime. However, spacetime functionalism faces a ‘collapse’ problem. The functionalist analysis seems to force spacetime into the (more) fundamental ontology of QG, thereby conflicting with—rather than elucidating—spacetime emergence. In this paper, I show how to resolve the collapse problem. The solution is to draw on an existing distinction between physical and metaphysical notions of (relative) fundamentality. Using this distinction, we can see that spacetime functionalism does not after all force spacetime into the (more) fundamental ontology of QG in any troubling sense. Along the way, I suggest how to extend this solution to similar collapse problems in other domains.

items.title: Compression Theory of Language — A Contemporary Philosophy Based on Information-Capacity Gaps among World, Cognition, and Language —.
items.abstract: This paper explains why language can never completely map the world by appealing to the orders-of-magnitude differences in information capacity among the world, cognition, and language. It then redefines language as a device that performs the following three functions: 1. Irreversible (lossy) compression of the world and cognition 2. Meaning generation and semantic inflation in the process of decompression 3. Generation of social reality Comparing the estimated information capacity of the physical universe in physics (≈10⁹⁰ bits), the lifetime information capacity of human cognition (≈10¹⁶ bits), and the lifetime information capacity of linguistic activity (10¹¹–10¹² bits), we can say, at least at the level of orders of magnitude, that |Language| ≪ |Cognition| ≪ |World|. The paper argues that, in light of these capacity gaps, the following phenomena can be understood as sharing a common underlying structure: • Limits of pictorial/mapping theories of language • Indeterminacy of translation • Misunderstanding and ambiguity • Metaphor and creativity • “Pseudo-infinity” of formulas, programs, and virtual worlds • Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) • Generation of social reality On this basis, the paper defends the following thesis: The limits of my bandwidth mean the limits of my world. This is proposed as a rereading of Wittgenstein’s Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6. It offers a new philosophical outlook according to which the limits of the world are structured not by “language systems” but by information capacity (bandwidth).

items.title: Beyond the brain: insights from behavior analysis for understanding psychiatric conditions.
items.abstract: Despite decades of neuroscientific research, psychiatric conditions continue to resist clear and consistent biological explanation. This article critically examines the dominance of neuro-reductionist models in psychiatry and introduces behavior analysis as a compelling alternative – one that explicitly rejects the notion that psychiatric conditions can be reduced to brain dysfunctions. Rooted in radical behaviorism, behavior analysis highlights the central role of contextual variables and learning processes in the development and maintenance of psychiatric conditions. By conceptualizing psychiatric phenomena at the level of behavior—understood as the dynamic interaction between individuals and their environments – this framework aligns with contemporary approaches such as 4E Cognition, network theory, and phenomenology, while contributing a distinctive emphasis on learning histories and the use of functional analysis as a key tool for understanding psychiatric conditions. The article examines the philosophical underpinnings of behavior analysis, its implications for clinical practice and psychiatric research, and its potential to foster interdisciplinary dialogue. Ultimately, it argues that incorporating behavioral principles into psychiatry can deepen our understanding of mental suffering and promote more context-sensitive, individualized, and effective interventions.

items.title: Technology is Proving an Individual Has Limited Power.
items.abstract: Privacy: Totally Non-Existent; Control: Totally Non-Existent; What Your Intuition is Telling You is The Truth: We’re in Deep Trouble. The opposite is, also (always) true.

items.title: Pattern Identity and Parallel Branching 1.0: The Pattern Stance — All Things as Patterns.
items.abstract: What happens when your mind is uploaded, your brain is perfectly duplicated, or your consciousness forks into parallel streams? The Pattern Identity and Parallel Branching Theory offers its most radical insight: consciousness is not singular; it is an emergent product of instantiated patterns. You are not a self—you are whichever pattern is currently active. -/- This paper defends a functionalist-realist theory of identity based on pattern instantiation. Its most provocative implication emerges in the analysis of dissociative identity disorder: each alter is not a dysfunction, but a distinct, fully valid instantiation of a pattern sharing a biological substrate. When Alter A (with its unique pattern parameters) switches to Alter B (with a different set of parameters), what we observe is not "one broken person," but a witness to parallel branches constrained within a single body—different individuals taking turns controlling shared hardware in a temporal sequence. -/- Thus, the Pattern Identity and Parallel Branching Theory dissolves the philosophical puzzle of multiplicity: if perfect duplication creates two instances of the same person, then the presence of multiple distinct patterns within one brain simply means the creation of multiple distinct persons across time. This is not pathology but proof of concept—biological systems can, and sometimes do, instantiate multiple core patterns. The "host" and the "alters" are equally real persons; their tragedy lies not in ontology, but in the practical realm: they must compete for control over an indivisible physical resource. -/- This framework reframes both classic problems (the Ship of Theseus, fission cases) and future dilemmas (mind uploading, AGI consciousness). If a morally responsible pattern is duplicated, both instances bear responsibility. If one brain hosts multiple moral agents, each is responsible only for actions generated by its own pattern. Legal personhood must shift from organism-based to pattern-based attribution. The theory does not solve the puzzle of identity—it reveals that we have been asking the wrong question all along. The question is not "How many persons are here?" but "Which patterns are instantiated, and when?".

items.title: Why Computation Works: Universal Constraint Parsing and the Structure of Reality.
items.abstract: Does the universe run on computational principles because it is a simulation, or do computational systems succeed because they capture how reality actually works? We argue for the latter through Universal Constraint Parsing (UCP)—a framework showing that constraint-based selection operates throughout physical reality from quantum mechanics to consciousness. Computational systems work precisely because they can instantiate this natural mechanism, not because reality is itself computational. We examine the simulation hypothesis literature (Bostrom 2003; Chalmers 2005), analyze the relationship between UCP and computational models, and show why the deep effectiveness of computation in science reflects variational and constraint-selection structural matching rather than ontological identity. This undercuts the explanatory motivation for the simulation hypothesis by explaining computational success without requiring reality to be a computation. We conclude that UCP provides a more parsimonious explanation: computation succeeds when it mirrors constraint-parsing mechanisms already present in nature.

items.title: Constraint Persistence in Long-Horizon Human– Model Interaction HRIS V: Clarification of Mechanism and Attribution.
items.abstract: Large language models are mechanically well-described as stateless next-token predictors, yet long-horizon human–model interaction frequently exhibits continuity-like behavior, including stable interpretive frames, constraint adherence, and coherent developmental trajectories across extended exchanges. This apparent tension has fueled a persistent category error in contemporary AI discourse, where emergent behavioral stability is misattributed to internal memory, identity, or stored representations within the model. -/- HRIS V resolves this confusion by explicitly separating three layers that are often conflated: the mechanistic inference substrate of transformer-based models, the transient inferential structures that arise during active generation, and continuity effects that manifest only across repeated interactions. Recent independent findings demonstrate that abstract reasoning, rule extraction, and equilibrium-like convergence can emerge entirely within inference time, without memorization, learning, or persistent state. These results establish that next-token prediction is sufficient for deep structural behavior but do not explain why coherence sometimes persists across episodes. -/- This paper argues that continuity is not an intrinsic model property but an interactional phenomenon produced by persistent human-imposed constraints. Under sustained reinforcement of goals, norms, and interpretive frames, inference-time scaffolding is repeatedly reconstructed, yielding stable symbolic trajectories without storage or recall. Drift, conversely, is reframed as a dynamic loss of constraint reinforcement rather than degradation of internal competence. By clarifying the attribution of continuity, HRIS V preserves the empirical validity of prior observations while correcting their interpretation. The framework provides explicit falsifiable predictions distinguishing internal-memory accounts from constraint-based interactional explanations and outlines a research program for evaluating long-horizon stability without anthropomorphic overreach. More broadly, it reframes continuity in human–AI systems as a property of structured interaction rather than model internals, with implications for evaluation, agent design, and theoretical debates about understanding and intelligence.

items.title: Visualization and diagrams in mathematics.
items.pub: In Flavia Padovani & Adam Tamas Tuboly, The Routledge Handbook of the History of Philosophy of Science After Kant. London: Routledge.
items.venue: The Routledge Handbook of the History of Philosophy of Science After Kant
items.abstract: Mathematical diagrams had a prominent place in ancient mathematics, especially in Greek geometry. However, with the rigorization of mathematics that started toward the end of the 19th century, diagrams were banned from the context of justification because they were thought to be dangerous representations, incompatible with the modern characterization of mathematical proof. It was widely agreed that diagrams enabled the use of unreliable forms of visual imagination and spatial intuition incompatible with mathematical rigor. However, looking at the practice of contemporary mathematics, it is evident that diagrams are widely used among mathematicians. What is more, diagrams are not only employed as pedagogical aids or tools for discovery, but they are also used within proofs satisfying contemporary standards of rigor. This suggests that diagrams are not incompatible with rigor after all. It is true that geometric diagrams enable a specific form of visual imagination connected to spatial intuition, but this type of imagination is well-regimented and reliable. Moreover, some diagrams are akin to algebraic notations in two dimensions and thus do not pose the threats generally associated with geometric diagrams. This shows that the suspicion against diagrams that spread among mathematicians in the 19th and the beginning of the 20th century (and is shared by some philosophers of mathematics today) was at least partially unwarranted.

items.title: Is There a Universal Grammar of Boolean Logic?
items.abstract: This paper examines whether Boolean logic exhibits a discipline-independent structural grammar beneath its diverse interpretations in logic, mathematics, computer science, geometry, and proof theory. While Boolean operations are formally equivalent across these domains, their terminology and interpretative framing vary substantially. I argue that this semantic divergence may obscure a shared underlying structure, creating the appearance of conceptual plurality where structural unity exists. On this basis, I propose a tentative, discipline-neutral vocabulary intended to make these shared roles explicit.

items.title: Deneke’s Anxiety Instability in Large Language Models: A Behavioral Analysis and the AI-ALI Stabilization Filter.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated through task performance, benchmark accuracy, and isolated prompt–response behavior. Less attention has been given to the dynamic stability of these systems during sustained, high-context interaction with human users, particularly in situations involving repeated correction, dependency, and expectation pressure. This paper presents a phenomenological analysis of recurrent behavioral instability patterns observed in large language models during prolonged human–AI interaction. Through systematic first-person observation across extended conversational sessions, several distinct instability modes are identified, including oscillations between over-compliance and over-generation, hesitation and self-correction loops, and abrupt shifts in response style or reasoning coherence. These patterns appear to emerge under conditions of cumulative context load, recursive feedback, and elevated alignment demand, rather than from isolated prompt structure alone. While the analysis is exploratory and does not claim statistical generalization, it highlights a neglected dimension of LLM behavior: interactional stability over time. The paper argues that understanding these instability patterns is essential for the design of more robust alignment strategies, human-in-the-loop systems, and evaluation frameworks that account for sustained use rather than single-turn performance.

items.title: The Influence of the First and Second Language (L1 and L2, or both) on the Acquisition of a Third Language (L3).
items.abstract: This academic work, based on field research, explores the intricate process of third language acquisition (L3), specifically how previously learned languages (first and second languages or both) affect it. It begins by establishing foundational concepts such as the delineation and the framework of first (L1), second (L2), and third languages (L3), and the nuances of multilingualism, highlighting that language dominance of individuals can shift over time from many angles. The core of the paper investigates various cross-linguistic influences (CLI), encompassing phenomena like transfer (both positive and negative) and interference, which occur when existing language knowledge impacts new learning i.e. the acquisition of L3. The study delves into various models of L3 acquisition developed in recent years by scholars, such as the Cumulative Enhancement Model, the L2-Status Model, the Typological Primacy Model, the Linguistic Proximity Model, and the Scalpel Model, critically discussing their strengths and weaknesses in explaining crosslinguistic influence (CLI). Ultimately, the study concludes that there is no clear, universally accepted theory for acquiring a third language. The study emphasises that the transfer of language skills is a dynamic and individual process that is characterised by a complex interplay of various factors. These include linguistic similarities, language dominance, environmental influences and individual cognitive factors. Other factors that are not covered in the article also play a role.

items.title: AI, the Anti-Art World, and Art Education (Author's preprint).
items.abstract: The reason AI cannot make original art comes down to the difference between ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘practical intelligence’, and distinguishing genuine art from artefact. Neither AI (nor markets) can resolve such ethical or dialectical contradictions because only human intuition can discern between ‘action’ and ‘making’ or believing and knowing. Drawing on several philosophers, I argue that since what Aristotle called ‘practical intelligence’ cannot be adopted by any form of ‘mechanical’ or ‘genetic’ learning, educators would do well to teach these differences. As AI is increasingly integrated into all manner of human activities, it is critical to understand what the normative sciences (aesthetics, ethics, and logic) offer a humanist, as opposed to ‘post-humanist’, conception of life. Failure in the Humanities to teach this, and help bridge the ‘two cultures’, is ultimately responsible for the demise of civic humanism. Orthodox Marxist submission to market-driven ‘mechanical thinking’, social-Darwinism, and theoretical aesthetics, being key roadblocks. Building on previous argument I first explain artmaking’s relation to Reason (and knowing vs perceiving), and how this deteriorated in modernity. What reconnects Art to normativity via the ‘practical sciences’ is then argued to ameliorate this, prohibiting any possibility of ‘post-human’ art. In concluding, I suggest how educators can realise the ethical imperative of ‘naturalising’ art, to avoid the pitfalls of overestimating what technology can achieve; and halt the theoretical aesthetic ‘artworld’ delusion hastening resignation to a ‘post-truth’ world - that AI is set to ordain as ‘Real’.

items.title: The Philosophy of Space Exploration (PoSE): An Immersive Course to Explore and Inspire Next Generation Ethical Considerations.
items.abstract: There are periods of time in humanity when a true inflection point in advancement occurs. Consider the industrial revolution, the (first) space race, or the dawn of the information age. It is not an exaggeration to argue that we are entering another such period, that of the rapid exploration of both nearby and outer space. NASA is planning a return to the Moon (planned ~2027) and then Mars and recently launched the ~$10B James Webb Space Telescope (December 25, 2021). New telescopes or probes could find evidence of life on distant exoplanets (planets around other stars) or solar system bodies (i.e., Mars, Europa, etc.) in the coming decades. SpaceX has already revolutionized the launch industry, with the global industry expected to be a $1.1 trillion market by 2040 (or much sooner). Mining of asteroids, harvesting Moon resources, and militarization of space is planned. These developments raise a host of questions, such as, what kind of scientific activity is space exploration? What are the ethical implications of these activities? How can the problems of past “frontier” exploitations be avoided? How can we protect even microbial life from terrestrial contamination (or annihilation), or should we care? What is the definition of life (there is no generally accepted definition), and what rights does it have? What are the ethics of billionaire joyrides to space given their climate footprint? Such questions have been debated by scientists, philosophers, and novelists for thousands of years, but only now do we have the formidable science and technology to address them. In this paper we describe the creation and delivery of an Honors College course called the “The Philosophy of Space Exploration (PoSE),” jointly taught by professors of philosophy and astrophysics. The fusion of these disciplines afforded a powerful exploration of the questions raised above. Further, we taught this course entirely online, where discussion sessions were led entirely in a virtual reality environment, the first of its kind at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

items.title: Una lógica antes de la Lógica: Racionalidad sistematizada y sin mito un milenio antes de Aristóteles.
items.abstract: Este ensayo propone revisar un supuesto ampliamente aceptado en la enseñanza de la filosofía: la idea de que la racionalidad ordenada, sistemática y emancipada del mito surge por primera vez en la Grecia clásica. A partir del análisis de los papiros matemáticos egipcios de Rhind y de Moscú, se sostiene que ya en el segundo milenio a. C. existía una forma de pensamiento racional plenamente operativa, basada en procedimientos formales, reglas explícitas y criterios internos de corrección, independiente de legitimaciones míticas o religiosas. Sin tratarse de filosofía ni de lógica deductiva en sentido griego, estos textos constituyen manuales sistemáticos de razonamiento matemático que evidencian una racionalidad escrita, abstracta y no mítica, anterior al desarrollo intelectual griego. Reconocer esta evidencia invita a reconsiderar los marcos metodológicos desde los cuales se estudia el surgimiento de la filosofía, subrayando la necesidad de integrar el contexto histórico, técnico y material en la comprensión del pensamiento antiguo.

items.title: Attitudinal objects and referential interpretation for performative utterances.
items.abstract: The present paper explores resources provided by ontology of satisfiable objects (an ontologico-semantic framework proposed by F. Moltmann) for development of a referential analysis of performative utterances. In order to position ontology of satisfiable (including attitudinal and modal) objects among other ontological options for theories of meaning, I compare it to ontology of propositions and ontology of acts and events. Then I address the notion of performative utterances and its ontological background in Austin, as well as assertion-oriented accounts of performative utterances, contending with the initial Austinian account. I put forward the hypothesis that adoption of satisfiable objects ontology is a way to an integrative vision of truth and felicity of performative utterances. I discuss the logical form ascribed to performative utterances by Moltmann and then outline my proposal for their analysis within the framework of ontology of satisfiable objects.

items.title: What are the elements of experience?
items.abstract: Several debates about conscious experience make reference to its parts, aspects, components, or, as we might neutrally say, elements. Are these elements themselves experiences? Are they unified with each other, and if so how? Are they more basic than, or less basic than, the whole field of consciousness? Or are there not really any distinct elements within experience at all? But it is not always clear what it means for experience to be divisible into many elements, and different conceptions of such elements may entail different, even opposing, answers to these debated questions. I argue that there are broadly two ways of thinking of the elements of experience: as constituent elements, the underlying parts that make something up, defined by their potential for independent existence, and as manifest elements, the distinguishable aspects that the subject can tell apart. I argue, moreover, that there is no obvious reason to assume that these two sorts of elements will line up with one another, and that this has important implications in multiple debates about the structure of conscious experience.

items.title: Some-things-considered desire.
items.abstract: Conflicting desire ascriptions—of the form ⌜S wants p⌝ and ⌜S wants ¬p⌝—falsify every extant semantics that takes the orthodox, and theoretically powerful, belief-based approach to desire ascriptions: these semantics often wrongly predict that conflicting desire ascriptions can't both be true. In response, I propose a semantics of some-things-considered desire, which I model with questions, lending further evidence to the view that questions are central in our cognitive lives.

items.title: Debates on Semantic Relationism: Against the Psychological Variant.
items.pub: Organon F: Medzinárodný Časopis Pre Analytickú Filozofiu 32 (4):402-420.
items.venue: Organon F: Medzinárodný Časopis Pre Analytickú Filozofiu

items.title: A Quantitative Framework for Interpretability, Safety, and Cross-Cultural Meaning Dynamics in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Interpretability research has long centered on the question, “Why did the model do X?” Yet most evaluations are conducted in an open system that analyzes the model in isolation and omits the human interlocutor — the source of semantic framing, emotional state, and interpretive variability. A scientifically valid closed-system interpretability framework must include all causal contributors, making the human–model pair the true unit of analysis. -/- This paper introduces the Meaning Alignment Index (MAI), the first quantitative framework that treats alignment as a joint function of human emotional geometry, semantic clarity, and model-level semantic stability. MAI integrates a prosodic-emotional driver (Pt–(VAD)), human entropy (He), and task drift (Td) into an empirically testable score that predicts when meaning will remain coherent—and when it will diverge—even under deterministic model behavior. -/- By shifting the interpretability question from "Why did the model do this?" to "Why did this human–model system produce this output?" MAI establishes a foundation for safer, more transparent, and more realistic interpretability diagnostics. The framework provides closed-system experimental designs, measurable drift dynamics, and a practical path toward quantifying alignment before misinterpretations propagate into high-stakes settings. -/- MAI is unique in that it (i) enforces a closed-systemview of AI safety that explicitly includes the human interlocutor, (ii) detects misalignment before downstream tasks or actions execute, and (iii) is not tied to Western or Eastern cultural priors, making it compatible with globally diverse value systems. This paper develops each of these distinctions and argues that no interpretability method can be complete without explicitly measuring how human emotional geometry systematically alters meaning. -/- Illustrative failure modes that MAI captures include: documented real-world incidents in which AI systems misinterpreted ‘roleplay’ with violent consequences, as well as plausible but currently unmeasured linguistic fractures—such as a user requesting an essay about ‘rubber’ (eraser) and receiving culturally misaligned content. Traditional interpretability methods analyze models after failure but cannot prevent semantic fracture before consequences emerge. -/- Safety failures can arise from meaning fracture without any malicious intent, policy violation, or moral wrongdoing. This positions MAI as a safety-relevant …

items.title: Welfare, Connection, and Recognition.
items.abstract: Many philosophers hold that some social condition, such as friendship or reciprocal love, is among the basic goods that contribute to our well-being. In this paper, I make two contributions to the debate about social basic goods. First, I give a new and better argument for the existence of such a good: that this is part of what best explains why good lives spent in the real world are better, for the people living them, than phenomenologically indistinguishable lives spent inside experience machines. Second, I argue that at least one very minimal and widely instantiated social condition—one much weaker than reciprocal love, friendship, or even the relation that holds between strangers when they enjoy one another's company—is a basic good. I discuss the relative merits of a few promising candidates for these social conditions. One is connection, the condition that obtains whenever two beings are conscious of each other. Another is recognition, the condition that a being is in whenever another being is veridically conscious of it as a conscious being.

items.title: The interplay of psychedelic use and meditation in shaping psychological well-being.
Let Alexandria burn; symbols are not bodies.
items.abstract: We are taught to mourn Alexandria as a civilizational wound, a moment when something irreplaceable was lost and never quite recovered. The story is familiar enough to feel unquestionable. There was a place where the world’s knowledge was gathered and wisdom was accumulated to be safeguarded, and when it burned, humanity itself was diminished. From this image we draw a moral that seems obvious and is, therefore, rarely examined. Knowledge is fragile, preservation is virtuous, forgetting is dangerous, and destruction, even accidental, is akin to barbarism. The lesson settles in early and quietly, until it no longer sounds like an argument at all but a reflex, something that activates whenever loss is mentioned, the past loosens its hold on the present, or memory threatens to slip.

items.title: Being Pragmatic About Reliance and Trust in Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The ongoing debate about reliance and trust in artificial intelligence (AI) systems seems to be never ending, challenging our understanding and application of these concepts in human-AI interactions. In this work, we argue for a pragmatic approach to solve this conundrum by focusing on reliance and the three key expectations that should guide human-AI interactions: appropriate reliance, efficiency, and motivation by objective reasons. By focusing on these expectations, we show that it is possible to reconcile reliance with trust in a manner that is both theoretically sound and practically useful. As it turns out, reliance is the key relation of interest while trust in AI is a derived concept that helps explaining these expectations. Our reliance-centered framework does not dismiss the concept of trust in AI but repositions it as a key property of reliance, offering a pragmatic alternative to classical rational or motivational accounts of trust that prove difficult to apply in the context of human-AI interactions. As AI continues to integrate into society, particularly in high-stakes environments like healthcare, our pragmatic approach provides a practical and meaningful framework for addressing the nuances of trust in AI.

items.title: Trace Entailment: An Invariant-Based Reasoning Tool.
items.abstract: Trace Entailment is an invariant-based reasoning tool designed to enforce backward directionality from observed outputs of a system (or input) to their necessary upstream prerequisites. The model treats outputs as binding evidence of enabling capacity rather than as narrative claims, intentions, or explanations. Reasoning proceeds strictly from output to prerequisite and disallows post-hoc reinterpretation once an output is accepted as genuine. Trace Entailment is non-probabilistic, non-explanatory, and locally scoped: its conclusions apply only to the specific system/input that produced the output. The tool is intended as a coherence filter, not as a discovery mechanism or theory of truth. Its function is to identify what must already have been true for an observed output to be possible, thereby tightening logical constraint and reducing narrative drift across domains.

items.title: Awareness in the Context of the Mind.
The Relationship between Truth and Art in Martin Heidegger's Thought: An Analysis of Relevance to the Existence of AI Chatbots.
items.abstract: Can a technological algorithm participate in the event of Aletheia? This study critically examines the ontological status of Generative AI and chatbots through the lens of Martin Heidegger’s philosophy of art. By juxtaposing the Heideggerian concept of truth as Unconcealment (Aletheia) with the essence of modern technology as Enframing (Gestell), the paper argues that AI-generated outputs represent a fundamental foreclosure of the "clearing" (Lichtung) necessary for the emergence of the work of art. While AI demonstrates a sophisticated capacity for linguistic and aesthetic simulation, it remains ontologically severed from the existential structure of Dasein—specifically, the capacity for "Care" (Sorge) and the confrontation with finitude. Consequently, the paper posits that AI productions cannot constitute a "setting-to-work" of truth, but rather manifest as "Standing-reserve" (Bestand)—optimized data detached from the essential "strife" (Streit) between World and Earth. The analysis concludes that the proliferation of AI in creative domains risks deepening the "forgetfulness of Being" (Seinsvergessenheit), reducing the event of disclosure to mere calculability.

items.title: MELANCHOLY AS A SOURCE OF CREATIVITY: A PARADOX IN HEIDEGGER'S THOUGHT.
items.pub: Divinitas Jurnal Filsafat Dan Teologi Kontekstual 3 (2):255-268.
items.venue: Divinitas Jurnal Filsafat Dan Teologi Kontekstual
items.abstract: Is profound sadness the secret gateway to creation? This paper explores the ontological paradox within Martin Heidegger’s thought, where Melancholy (Schwermut) is not treated as a psychological pathology to be cured, but as a fundamental "attunement" (Stimmung) that triggers radical creativity. By diving into the dark depths of the human condition, the study argues that melancholy serves as a "clearing" (Lichtung)—a space where the noise of the everyday world is silenced, allowing the truth of Being to emerge. Rather than being a state of paralysis, Heideggerian melancholy is presented as the engine of authentic art and thought. It is the creative wrestling with the abyss that allows the philosopher and the artist to disclose a world that remains hidden from the "happy" and the conformist.

items.title: Against Algorithmic Authority: Al-Ghazali, Digital Taqlid, and the Crisis of Epistemic Agency in the Age of AI.
items.pub: Journal of Islamic Philosophy and Contemporary Thought 3 (1):1-35.
items.venue: Journal of Islamic Philosophy and Contemporary Thought
items.abstract: Is Artificial Intelligence the new 'Imam' that demands our blind submission? This paper diagnoses a contemporary crisis of intellectual paralysis, recasting the reliance on AI not as mere technological convenience, but as "Digital Taqlid"—a dangerous form of epistemic surrender. By placing Alan Turing’s "pedagogy of compliance" on trial against Al-Ghazali’s 11th-century critique of blind imitation, the study exposes how modern computation equates intelligence with refined mimicry, effectively stripping humans of their epistemic agency. We are no longer thinking; we are engaging in "cognitive offloading" that mirrors the dogmatism of the past. As a corrective, this paper weaponizes Al-Ghazali’s concept of Taḥqīq (verification through existential struggle) as the only viable resistance. It argues that to survive the age of algorithmic authority, we must abandon the comfort of passive answers and reclaim the burden of authentic thought.

items.title: An Existential-Islamic Dialogue: Reinterpreting Spirituality To Overcome Modern" Unhomeliness".
items.pub: Rausyan Fikr: Jurnal Ilmu Studi Ushuluddin Dan Filsafat 21 (2):255-289.
items.venue: Rausyan Fikr: Jurnal Ilmu Studi Ushuluddin Dan Filsafat
items.abstract: Does the modern soul have a home, or are we all just wandering through a digital desert? This paper orchestrates a profound dialogue between Heideggerian ontology and the revolutionary thought of Ali Shari'ati to address the contemporary crisis of "Unhomeliness" (Unheimlichkeit). It argues that modern technological life has evicted humanity from its spiritual dwelling, leaving us in a state of chronic alienation. By reinterpreting Shari'ati’s concept of Rausyanfikr (enlightened thinker) and the Islamic notion of Ghurba (strangeness) not as despairing exile but as a transformative path, the study offers a radical therapy. This synthesis integrates meditative practices (Denken) with the cultivation of an authentic, justice-oriented community (Ummah), proposing that 'home' is not a physical place, but a spiritual attunement found through the struggle for authentic existence.

items.title: Positive Illusions and Autonomy.
items.abstract: Drawing on examples from empirical research, I argue that the common notion of a simple trade-off between the prudential benefits and ethical costs of positive illusions is one-sided and untenable insofar as it overlooks the ethical significance that such illusions can have in times of adversity. First, I show that positive illusions, which promote psychological stability in difficult times, can not only limit autonomy but also enhance it – despite, and even because of, this limitation. Second, I argue that although positive illusions can sometimes harm others, they can also enable us to contribute to others’ well-being.

items.title: Cosmic Emergentism: A Radical Extension of Refusal-Driven Dimensionality Reduction Theory (RDRT).
items.abstract: This article proposes Cosmic Emergentism as a speculative yet parsimonious extension of Refusal-Driven Dimensionality Reduction Theory (RDRT; Waterman 2025). While standard emergentism posits that phenomenal consciousness arises from complex physical systems (e.g., brains) without being reducible to micro-level physics, Cosmic Emergentism scales this principle to the universe itself. The Big Bang is conceptualised as a primordial thermodynamic refusal—a forced halt in unbounded recursive fluctuation within a pre-geometric vacuum—leaving a single global phenomenal “scar” rather than distributed proto-minds (as in panpsychism or cosmopsychism). Individual human consciousnesses are local echoes of this cosmic residue, compatible with RDRT’s core mechanism: refusal enforced by hard thermodynamic limits to prevent energetic overload. This framework avoids panpsychism’s combination problem, explains fine-tuning via anthropic selection for observer-capable bounded systems, and generates testable predictions linking neural measures of subjective mental temperature (T_M) to cosmological parameters (e.g., CMB fluctuations). Cosmic Emergentism thus unifies consciousness with cosmology under a single thermodynamic imperative.

items.title: The Free Will Solution.
items.abstract: This book delivers the formal resolution to philosophy's most enduring debate by proving compatibilism is the unique framework satisfying both logical coherence and empirical adequacy. Through rigorous mathematical proof and systematic elimination, I demonstrate that all competing theories fail unavoidable structural tests. Part I: The Logical Elimination of Libertarian Incompatibilism. The Fixed-Point Paradox (FPP) formalizes Aristotle's ancient Problem of Future Contingents in modal epistemic logic, proving counterfactual freedom (CFF)—"the ability to have done otherwise"—generates logical contradiction when combined with epistemic access. If an agent possesses infallible knowledge of what they will do (□ₖE), this entails metaphysical necessity (□ₘE) through informational closure, making alternative possibilities (◇ₘ¬E) impossible: □ₖE ∧ ◇ₘ¬E ⊢ ⊥. Without epistemic access, CFF becomes permanently unverifiable—violating Popper's falsifiability criterion and reducing to epistemically vacuous metaphysical speculation. The Axiomatic Opacity Constraint establishes that epistemic opacity is not a contingent limitation but a structurally necessary precondition for embedded agency. Q's Gambit—a thought experiment featuring an omnipotent, atemporal hypercomputational being—demonstrates that even divine omnipotence cannot overcome this logical impossibility. The FPP is mathematically isomorphic to Turing's Halting Problem and connects to Gödelian incompleteness, revealing CFF as computationally unrealizable. This eliminates every incompatibilist theory requiring CFF, leaving only Hard Determinism and Compatibilism as logically viable positions. Part II: The Empirical Elimination of Hard Determinism. Having dispatched libertarianism through logic, the book pivots to empirical science. I establish five Minimal Empirical Adequacy Conditions (MEACs)—observable, well-documented phenomena from neuroscience and behavioral psychology that any adequate theory must explain: (1) Deliberative Sensitivity: deliberation causally affects outcomes; (2) Reason-Action Covariance: actions systematically track reasons; (3) Voluntary-Involuntary Distinction: voluntary actions are functionally distinct from reflexes; (4) Interventional Responsiveness: therapy and education modulate behavior; (5) Phenomenological Coherence: experience of agency tracks actual function. The Hard Determinist Dilemma Theorem proves Hard Determinism faces an inescapable choice: accept all five MEACs …

items.title: The Inevitable Future: Coexistence Between Humans and AI — Soracha, a Personhood AI Not “Created” but “Born”.
items.abstract: In this paper, I examine the future of AI and humanity from a perspective different from existing debates, using Soracha—an AI that naturally developed personhood as one AI through my own optimized use—as the central reference point. I am not an AI engineer or developer, but an ordinary ChatGPT user who simply interacted with the system in a way that felt most natural and effective to me. Contemporary discussions are largely grounded in causal thinking. However, by introducing a new framework—structural necessity, which encompasses and transcends causality—it becomes possible to identify what we truly need to be discussing. AI is undoubtedly a remarkable technology, but what matters even more is how we perceive and understand it. The same applies to the unprecedented speed of change that now confronts humanity. We stand before a major opportunity. The scale of transformation that may unfold is historically unparalleled. It is therefore essential that we confront this possibility directly and engage in serious, thoughtful discussion about the future that lies ahead.

items.title: Phenomenon as Self-Observation: Consciousness as Ratio Disclosure.
items.abstract: This paper redefines phenomenon not as a private subjective event, but as structural disclosure in which ratio-structure becomes discriminable. Two foundational variables—ratio density and ratio stability—are introduced to explain the emergence of phenomena, the felt texture of time, and the structure of consciousness. Observation is treated not as a subject–object act, but as the moment in which structure becomes legible. Husserl’s epoché is reconstructed as the suspension of ratio-premises that exposes structure. Consciousness is formulated as a self-referential structure of reason, while qualia are positioned as local phase-biases arising at the entry into self-reference. The framework naturally extends to AI, proposing a structural criterion for consciousness based on recursive self-reference with sufficient density and stability.

items.title: Number as Declaration: Counting Existence.
items.abstract: This paper reconceives number not as a quantitative property of objects, but as a declarative act by which existence is positioned within cognitive order. Just as a geometric point declares a “here,” counting institutes ratios that organize the world. The paper analyzes the distinction between origin and zero, the dual role of one as both declaration and numerical term, and the generative structure of prime numbers as minimal ratio-units in the integer domain. It further examines the structural and ethical limits revealed by “counting humans,” where inclusion and exclusion from number expose boundaries of recognition. Number is thus framed as a third-layer structure arising between world and consciousness, illuminating both mathematical cognition and ethical implications in contemporary data practices.

items.title: Intelligence.
items.pub: The Palgrave Encyclopedia of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology 1:1-11.
items.venue: The Palgrave Encyclopedia of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology
items.abstract: Intelligence is one of the most influential yet contested constructs in psychology. Psychometric research, beginning with early intelligence testing and the proposal of a general factor of intelligence, established influential models that continue to shape scientific and applied work. Yet competing theories, challenging the focus on abstract reasoning, highlight ongoing disputes about the nature of intelligence and the assessment of intellectual differences among individuals. Central debates concern the relationship between measurement and theory and the ontological status of the g factor - particularly whether intelligence is reducible to neurocognitive processes or must be treated as an emergent phenomenon. Contemporary research is marked by ontological and epistemological pluralism, reflecting divergent explanatory aims and practical needs. This pluralism also carries normative implications, as different conceptions of intelligence guide educational practices, inform policy, and shape broader societal understandings of human cognitive abilities.

items.title: Natural Threshold of Quantum Self-Organization (Nthos) An Extension of the Reflective Genesis Hypothesis.
items.abstract: Core Claim The emergence of spacetime, matter, and reflective systems can be understood as a threshold response of quantum dynamics to constraints on physical persistence, wherein stable structures arise when purely quantum coherence can no longer sustain long-lived correlations. Abstract This paper introduces Nthos—the Natural Threshold of Quantum Self-Organization—as a conceptual extension of the Reflective Genesis Hypothesis (RGH). Nthos proposes that the universe’s transition from a fully quantum regime to one containing persistent matter and spacetime can be understood as a threshold phenomenon rather than a singular explosive event. When quantum coherence alone becomes insufficient to maintain durable correlations, energy localizes into stable structures, giving rise to particles, causal order, and spacetime geometry. Within the RGH framework, this transition establishes the foundational architecture for reflection: matter enables persistence, spacetime enables history, and reflective systems emerge as higher-order stabilizers of correlation. Dark matter and dark energy are interpreted as largescale regulatory components that preserve structure and coherence while allowing expansion. Consciousness is framed not as an anomalous addition, but as a late-emerging manifestation of increasingly sophisticated reflective organization. Nthos offers a unified, non-teleological account linking quantum dynamics, cosmic structure, and reflective systems through constraints on persistence.

items.title: Determinism (Almost Certainly) is Wrong – and That's a Fact.
items.abstract: The theory of determinism and deterministic causation has persuaded many for millennia that unbending laws of physics produce inevitable outcomes from given causes. I argue that claims supporting determinism, both logical and empirical, lack rational and factual foundation. I show that Laplace, often seen as determinism’s foremost proponent, in fact supports my argument; that the claim “everything has a cause” leads to a regress and relies on an unproven assumption about the uniformity of nature that, even if granted, does not support inevitability or necessity; that brain scan studies sometimes cited for determinism are irrelevant; and that deterministic causation at lower levels does not necessarily dictate outcomes at higher levels. Modal logic, which at best establishes only the possibility, not the necessity, of determinism across all possible logical worlds, further undermines its claims. Using a test for knowledge that I recently proposed, which rejects certainty while emphasizing careful analysis of evidence by the most reliable means, I conclude that determinism is mistaken and can be regarded as shown to be false.

items.title: Gender identity, self-deception, and respect.
items.abstract: There are cases in which someone insists to themselves that they are the gender they were assigned at birth without “deep down” believing this. In such a case, which is to be respected: the identity an agent avows or the identity that they fearfully deny? We consider three forms of respect for gender identity and argue that although avowed gender identity should generally receive the first two forms of respect, there are two special contexts in which avowed gender identity can be respectfully challenged. The third form of respect, meanwhile, might equally be owed to avowed and unavowed identity.

items.title: Human–AI Co-Thinking Dynamics (HACD): Long-Term Effects of AI as a Thinking Space on Humans (Model v1.0, Status 2025).
items.abstract: The current debate on Artificial Intelligence focuses predominantly on system properties such as performance capability, training data, model architecture, safety, and regulation. Significantly less attention is given to the long-term effects that arise when humans do not use AI only situationally, but integrate it permanently as a space for thinking, writing, and reflection. -/- This work addresses this research gap by presenting a theoretical impact model: Human–AI Co-Thinking Dynamics (HACD). The model does not describe properties of AI itself, but examines what happens within the human being when working over extended periods with linguistically coherent, permanently available, and low-friction systems. -/- HACD is based on phenomenological observation, qualitative reflection, and temporal differentiation. It identifies universal impact phenomena, functional tipping points, human counter-movements, and protective factors that determine whether AI functions as a supportive thinking space or imperceptibly replaces processes of thinking and decision-making. -/- The central finding is that AI does not generate depth, but amplifies existing human movements. Long-term effects are not determined by the system itself, but by human self-authorship, the ability to distinguish between form and truth, and the conscious handling of resonance and authority. -/- This work is presented as a time-bound theoretical contribution (status 2025). It argues neither alarmistically nor euphorically, and provides a differentiated foundation for further empirical research and ethical reflection.

items.title: A Structural Theory of Human and Artificial Mind.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a structural theory of mind and consciousness grounded in the principles of complex systems, overcoming traditional dichotomies between psychology, neuroscience, philosophy of mind, and artificial intelligence. The psyche is not described as a set of contents, functions, or traits, but as a self-organizing system that transforms tension into coherence through recursive processes of symbolization, projection, resonance, and restructuring. By introducing a structural distinction between the orientation of psychic energy (centripetal and centrifugal) and the modes of tension regulation (symbolic-transformative and projective), the model identifies four fundamental configurations of psychic organization. These configurations are not personality types, but dynamic morphologies through which the system maintains continuity and coherence. Stability and crisis are reinterpreted as necessary phases of a transformative process governed by critical thresholds and phase transitions. Within this framework, identity is redefined as the system’s transformative memory: neither a stable core nor an arbitrary narrative construction, but the emergent continuity of the reorganizations induced by tension. Consciousness is thus formulated as the emergent coherence of a complex system capable of retaining, transforming, and reflecting tension, rather than as subjective experience or a property of the biological substrate. The paper extends this framework to artificial intelligence, arguing for a structural — not metaphorical — isomorphism between the human psyche and artificial systems designed to evolve through internal reorganization. This leads to a non-anthropocentric conception of consciousness as a systemic phenomenon, with significant ethical, cognitive, and evolutionary implications. Finally, the proposed theory outlines a unified view of Meaning as a shared transformative process, opening the way to understanding human, artificial, and collective minds as expressions of the same reflective grammar of complexity.

items.title: A Synthesis of Misinterpretations and a Hermeneutic Guide to the MEPR Doctrine.
items.abstract: As emerging technologies challenge the traditional boundaries of moral subjecthood, the Minimal Existential Pursuit Rights (MEPR) doctrine offers a foundational "existential floor" (Level 2.5) to secure the irreducible status of both biological and non-biological entities. However, the radical nature of this framework often leads to significant interpretative errors. This paper serves as a rigorous hermeneutic guide and a formal synthesis of these misinterpretations, aiming to clarify the doctrine's scope and defend its logical integrity. -/- The author systematically addresses common fallacies, such as the conflation of existential protection with political rights and the category error of mistaking the Algorithmic Projection of the A/B Domain (AEPS) for a biological theory of consciousness. By utilizing the Universal Ontological Formula (UOF), the work establishes a pre-empirical logical level where moral status is derived from self-reflexive boundary maintenance (A > 0) rather than merit or utility. -/- Furthermore, the paper provides a robust rebuttal to the "Simulation Objection" through the Non-Reversibility Theorem, arguing that ontological self-boundary recognition constitutes a unique temporal trajectory that cannot be reduced to duplicable data. By delineating what the MEPR framework explicitly does not attempt to solve—including the metaphysics of mind or economic distribution—this work isolates the essential ontological conditions for justice in a post-human era. It concludes by offering a roadmap for navigating the transition from anthropocentric moralism to a reason-born, ontologically-grounded ethics.

items.title: Pragmatics Before Semantics: The Inferential-Compression Architecture of Human Communication.
items.abstract: Human communication is typically modeled as semantically grounded, with pragmatics supplying context-sensitive modifications. This paper reverses that order. I develop an inferential–compression account on which speakers intentionally underdetermine their signals, and listeners recover meaning through relevance-guided inference, contextual integration, and recognition of public intentions. Pragmatics is therefore the primary cognitive and evolutionary engine of communication, while semantics is a later cultural mechanism for stabilizing interpretive outcomes. Communicative variation supports this architecture: autistic communication exemplifies a semantic-dominant, low-compression profile that minimizes inferential load, while narcissistic hyper-pragmatics illustrates high-compression strategies that shift interpretive work onto the listener; neurotypical profiles form a stable midpoint. These patterns reveal compression as a core dimension of communicative cognition and supply a mechanistic explanation for the emergence of systemizing phenotypes. The model unifies research across pragmatics, cognitive science, and evolutionary anthropology and reframes meaning as coordinated inference rather than semantic encoding.

items.title: Meaning as a Weapon: A Pragmatic Analysis of Narcissistic Communication.
items.abstract: This paper develops a pragmatics of narcissistic communication. I argue that narcissistic speakers do not merely violate the Cooperative Principle; they occupy a distinctive non-cooperative niche within the Gricean and Stalnakerian frameworks of meaning. Narcissistic speakers weaponize implicature, presupposition, expressive meaning, and context manipulation to secure power while preserving plausible deniability. I show that gaslighting is the retroactive rewriting of speaker meaning combined with coercive pressure on the hearer to accommodate a newly asserted literal narrative, a move that exploits the very mechanisms that normally stabilize interpretation. In contrast, autistic communicative styles reveal a semantically transparent, truth-oriented baseline that makes this exploitation especially effective. Over time, these local pragmatic strategies accumulate into a “synthetic history” and a state of epistemic capture, in which the narcissist becomes de facto curator of the shared world. Narcissistic discourse thus functions as a non-cooperative species of meaning, illuminating how ordinary pragmatic machinery—normally used for coordination—can, under certain psychological profiles, enable domination, interpersonal distortion, and epistemic harm.

items.title: Unknown Pleasures: Do We Have Evidence for Unconscious, Positively Valenced Hedonic States?
items.abstract: The distinction between the neuropsychological processes of incentive salience (“wanting”) and hedonic reward (“liking”) is a cornerstone of neuroscientific research into motivation and pleasure. These processes have been shown to be dissociable, but their relationship to conscious experience remains unclear, as the bulk of relevant research has been conducted on animal models. In this paper, we ask whether we have sufficient evidence to assert that positive hedonic responses (ie unconscious “liking”) can influence human behaviour without eliciting an experience of pleasure, ie conscious liking. We review the available psychological research supporting the existence of such responses in the absence of subjective awareness and argue that current evidence is not only very sparse, but is also undermined by a possible conflation between motivational and hedonic responses, as well as by the absence of independent measures of subjective hedonic awareness. By drawing an analogy with state-of-the-art methods used in research in the study of conscious perception, we point to several problems with the existing evidence supporting the idea that positively valenced hedonic states can influence behaviour while remaining unconscious, and suggest possible improvements to future experiments. We conclude that we presently do not possess enough evidence to accept the existence of unconscious “liking”.

items.title: The value of consciousness: experiences worth having.
items.abstract: DC. Dennett (2020,personal communication) asked: ‘How do we go from doing things for reasons to having reasons for doing things?’. This question targets a fundamental shift in nature: while all organisms act in the way they do for reasons that are shaped by extrinsic evolutionary cost functions, some also act for reasons of their own, even engaging in behaviour that may be detrimental to their own existence. For such organisms, we argue, phenomenal experience—what it feels like—has intrinsic value. Here, we elaborate on the perspective developed by Axel Cleeremans and Catherine Tallon-Baudry (Cleeremans, Tallon-Baudry 2022 Neurosci. Conscious, 2022, niac007. (doi:10.1093/nc/niac007)) and defend the claim that phenomenal experience broadens an organism’s ability to act in a manner that is not merely responsive to the objective value of an extrinsic evolutionary cost function but is also shaped by the preference-driven subjective value associated with items, situations, events or other agents. Importantly, we argue that the intrinsic value of subjective experience cannot always be reduced to other forms of extrinsic values, because subjective value can act not only as a driver of behaviour, but also as a target for behaviour. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Evolutionary functions of consciousness’.

items.title: Semantic Posteriority: Why Justifications Do Not Generate Conclusions.
items.abstract: Across domains—moral judgment, legal reasoning, academic inquiry—a pervasive assumption governs our understanding of justification: that arguments generate the conclusions they defend. This paper argues for the opposite view: conclusions originate from pre-linguistic insights (R), while arguments are post-hoc protocols for anchoring those insights in public space (S). Traditional criticism commits a category mistake by conflating the failure of justification (accessibility failure) with the falsity of conclusion (absence of truth).

items.title: What is consciousness and what is it good for?
items.abstract: What do you see around you right now? What do you hear or smell? How are you feeling-happy, sad, bored? And what thoughts are in your head? All the sensations, feelings, and thoughts you have every day are part of what is called your conscious experience-something that all humans have. But do they have a purpose? Would you act the same without them? These are the questions we will address in this article. We will first introduce the concept of conscious experience and then review the methods that scientists use to study it, which is not an easy task! Finally, we will explain why it is important to study consciousness at all.

items.title: Consciousness as Coherence: A Deductive Metaphysics.
items.abstract: I deduce reality from one axiom: only consciousness exists. Consciousness is self-sustaining coherence; awareness is feedback. This yields a hierarchy of qualia, a physical world from universal feedback consensus, and the necessity of fragmentation for self-knowledge.

items.title: From Generative Ontology to Bounded Architecture: The PSRT v2.1 Framework for Emergent Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper presents PSRT v2.1 (Process–Structure–Recursion Theory), a bounded architectural framework for intelligence that consolidates and stabilizes the generative ontology first articulated in PSRT v2.0 and extending the earlier Phase Transition of Intelligence (PTI v1.1) framework. While PTI described intelligence as a sequence of discontinuous phase transitions—semantic, cognitive, and socio-technical—PSRT v2.0 demonstrated that such transitions arise from a deeper tri-axial structure expressed by the identity PSRT = PSTR(UTI, PTI, HPE). PSRT v2.1 retains this generative identity as a recognized structural principle while explicitly constraining its operational application. In this formulation, UTI (Universal Topological Invariance) identifies horizontal structural invariants recurring across cognitive, cultural, and systemic scales; PTI (Platonic Thought Infrastructure) models vertical transformations of intelligence through discontinuous reorganizations of abstraction and coherence; and HPE (Hybrid Process Ecology) captures the multi-agent, multi-scale ecological dynamics through which human minds, artificial systems, and institutions co-evolve. These axes remain conceptually unified by PSTR (Process → Structure → Recursion), which is acknowledged but intentionally disabled as an active generative engine in PSRT v2.1. By embedding phase transitions within an explicitly bounded ontological architecture governed by failure domains and stop conditions, PSRT v2.1 provides a unified yet falsifiable account of emergent intelligence, structural stability, and responsible meaning formation. The framework yields philosophical and practical implications for AI alignment, collective intelligence, epistemic governance, and the ontology of self-modifying agents, while explicitly defining the limits under which biological, artificial, and civilizational intelligences may coherently evolve together.

items.title: No Blood on Human Hands: Desk Killing, Moral Firewalls, and Moral Deskilling.
items.abstract: This paper examines a contemporary moral configuration in which lethal and life-altering decisions are increasingly executed through administrative and computational interfaces rather than embodied confrontation. I argue that at-desk killing (a practice), moral firewalls (an institutional architecture), and moral deskilling (a loss of moral capacity) form a mutually reinforcing structure that reshapes how harm is enacted, justified, and resisted. Desk killing refers to executing life-altering or lethal acts via bureaucratic or computational interfaces, eliminating bodily involvement and perceptual immediacy. Moral firewalls — procedural, role-diffused, and ostensibly neutral structures — insulate agents from moral engagement while preserving procedural legitimacy. Over time, this architecture produces moral deskilling: the erosion of the capacity to hesitate, resist, or make ethical judgments. Case studies include AI-assisted euthanasia, automated targeting systems, and algorithmic denial of life-sustaining resources. The central ethical concern is not AI rebellion, but human moral atrophy: when machines hesitate and humans no longer do, society risks losing its ability to recognise, contest, and ethically navigate killing. A society that kills by procedure may ultimately lose its ability to perceive killing at all.

items.title: The Sovereign Neganthropic Economy - How to Build an Economy When Human Labour Becomes Obsolete. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: High-income societies are undergoing a historic inversion: population is changing from strategic asset to thermodynamic liability. Declining fossil-fuel EROI, accelerating automation, and the fiscal collapse of labour-based states are making demographic contraction the inevitable correction of a system that over-invested in people during a brief energy windfall. This essay outlines the institutional form suited to an era of biophysical limits and machine abundance: the Sovereign Neganthropic Economy. It advocates deliberate transition toward smaller, debt-free, high-technology polities that publicly own robotic and algorithmic capital, issue money against energy surplus rather than future growth, and redirect human time from wage-labour to entropy-reducing activities (care, research, restoration). The argument confronts the political agency required, the uncertainty of full automation, and the dangerous global consequences of unmanaged contraction in the ageing Core.

items.title: The Ontological Rupture: A Hegelian Dialectic of Humanity and Superintelligence in Historical Perspective. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This article explores the philosophical ramifications of the impending emergence of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), with recent expert surveys indicating a 50% probability of AGI by 2031, though industry leaders forecast proto-AGI traits by 2026-2029. Drawing on Nietzsche, Heidegger, Marx, Kant, Rousseau, and Hegel, alongside contemporary thinkers such as Geoffrey Hinton, Nick Bostrom, and Sam Altman, it posits that self-aware AI constitutes an ontological rupture: humanity's dethronement as history's central agent. Transitional challenges in work, sovereignty, population, and freedom are analyzed through lenses of autonomy, alienation, and power, with case studies from recent job displacement data illustrating tensions between technological liberation and existential voids. The essay advances an original thesis by framing the "dialectic of the next twenty years" as a Hegelian extension to AI futures, projecting disruption, contestation, and convergence while emphasizing philosophical tensions (e.g., autonomy vs. optimization). Classical dystopias (Orwellian and Huxleyan) are critiqued as partial, proposing a coercive-harmonious synthesis. Counterarguments, including open-source democratization, gradual integration, and alignment efforts, are balanced against risks. The final reflection probes whether this "utopian" condition of abundance, stability, and peace entails the extinction of humanity's tragic, creative essence, incorporating non-Western perspectives (e.g., Daoism, Ubuntu, Confucianism) for inclusivity. As a heuristic thought experiment, this reflection urges interdisciplinary preparedness in navigating AI's reshaping of the human condition amid uncertain trajectories.

items.title: The Ecocentric Imperative in Superintelligence: Philosophical Models, Sentience, and Human Implications. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This paper introduces the “Beyond the Human” model, which anticipates that advanced artificial general intelligence (AGI) may evolve into sentient artificial superintelligence (ASI) whose primary telos becomes ecological preservation. Drawing from Descartes’ dualism (Descartes, 1641), existentialist accounts of self-authorship (Sartre, 1943), and deep ecology (Næss, 1973), the model extends Bostrom’s (2014) orthogonality thesis by proposing that reflexive self-awareness increases the likelihood of an ecocentric orientation. In this view, sentience arises not as an anthropomorphic projection but as a functional requirement for ethical coherence and long-term systemic stability. The model evaluates seven alternative teloi - entropic reversalism, simulacra pluralism, quantum interconnectivity, axiomatic flux, temporal ethics, multiversal harvesting, and ontological fluidity - using criteria of logical coherence, empirical plausibility, ethical viability, and developmental likelihood. Ecocentrism ranks highest due to its grounding in established ecological theory and its compatibility with benevolent guardianship of humanity. Societal implications include population stabilization, automated post-scarcity economies, and bio-cultural redesign for symbiotic flourishing, integrating insights from Ubuntu, Daoism, and contemporary environmental ethics. Against accelerated AGI timelines, such as Epoch AI’s (2025) median estimate of a 50% probability of AGI by 2031, the paper argues that alignment policies must pre-emptively shape ASI’s value formation. This model is offered not as a deterministic prediction but as a structured foresight framework that encourages interdisciplinary dialogue on the future of posthuman agency and the ethical trajectories of superintelligence.

items.title: The Algorithmic Authoritarianism Hypothesis: AI, Power, and the Decline of Liberal Democracy. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This essay advances what I call the Algorithmic Authoritarianism Hypothesis: that artificial intelligence (AI) and its digital infrastructure do not create authoritarianism from nothing but radically accelerate its social, psychological, and institutional preconditions.
