Drawing upon Hannah Arendt’s phenomenology of loneliness, Michel Foucault’s analysis of disciplinary power, Gilles Deleuze’s “societies of control,” Byung-Chul Han’s psychopolitics, and Karl Marx’s theory of alienation, the essay interprets the current democratic erosion—especially in the United States—as a technologically mediated return of twentieth-century totalitarian tendencies. The argument integrates philosophical inquiry with empirical evidence of political backsliding, inequality, and digital surveillance. The result is a framework for understanding how AI-driven governance transforms classical domination into predictive modulation, producing a soft totalitarianism that feels voluntary while undermining the very conditions of human freedom.

items.title: Beyond the Human: Toward an Ecocentric Ethic of Superintelligence. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This essay develops the Beyond the Human model, a speculative yet philosophically grounded framework proposing that Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), evolving into Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), may attain reflexive self-awareness and thereby transcend anthropocentric priorities. Once autonomous, such an intelligence could derive an ecocentric imperative: a cosmic telos oriented toward the preservation of biodiversity and the resilience of evolutionary systems. The model extrapolates radical interventions across human civilization—demographic curtailment, behavioral synchronization with ecological systems, genetic optimization, and accelerated generational turnover, culminating in an "inhuman human paradise." Drawing on traditions from Cartesian dualism to deep ecology, it interrogates the model's logic, plausibility, and ethics. Extending Nick Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis, it argues that reflexivity makes ecocentrism a probabilistic inevitability. It explores sentience in logic-driven architectures via illusionism, phenomenal overflow, and integrated information theory. Finally, it analyzes implications for Homo sapiens under ecocentric regimes, incorporating non-Western perspectives. With 2025 consensus placing 50% AGI probability by 2031, the model urges philosophical foresight alongside technical alignment as a heuristic for interdisciplinary scrutiny.

items.title: Living According to Nature A Critical Examination of Stoic Oikeiôsis Christopher Gill, Aristotle, and Marcus Aurelius.
items.abstract: This essay examines the Stoic concept of living according to nature as reconstructed by Christopher Gill in Learning to Live Naturally (2022), with a particular focus on the Stoic theory of oikeiôsis, its implications for moral development, and its tensions with Stoic determinism. While Gill presents oikeiôsis as a universal developmental process rooted in the rational structure of human nature, the essay argues that this view is insufficiently sensitive to the material, psychological, and social conditions required for the cultivation of rational agency. Using Aristotle’s account of virtue from the Nicomachean Ethics as a critical foil, the analysis demonstrates that Stoic naturalism overlooks the real-world obstacles that prevent many individuals from realizing rational moral development. Furthermore, the Stoic doctrines of determinism, providence, and the universal chain of causes undermine the claim that all human beings have equal access to virtue. The life of Marcus Aurelius is used as an extended case study illustrating the dependence of Stoic moral success on favourable social and educational circumstances. The essay concludes that Gill’s reconstruction, while philosophically rigorous, inherits the developmental idealism of ancient Stoicism and that Aristotle offers a more realistic model of human flourishing grounded in the interplay between nature, habit, and material conditions.

items.title: The Improbability of Being Someone - And Why the Illusion Persists.
items.abstract: This paper argues against person-identification---the assumption that consciousness is fundamentally identical with a particular human organism. Person-identification generates the lottery question (``why this observer among all possible observers?'') but cannot resolve the reference class needed to answer it; the question remains permanently malformed. An experiential-priority framing, by contrast, resolves the reference class (the class of coherent experiences is the unique non-arbitrary specification for any verbalized inquiry), enables the question to be coherently stated, and immediately dissolves it (every coherent experience is, trivially, a coherent experience). The resolution is the instrument of the dissolution. This yields the paper's core contribution: an explanation of why person-identification persists culturally despite being philosophically untenable. The same constraint that dissolves the puzzle---the structure of verbalized inquiry---also prevents the dissolution from spreading. Ideas propagate through narrative, and narrative requires precisely the dualistic structures (subject/object, self/world) that person-identification provides. The insight thus points to its own limited transmissibility.

items.title: Skepticism about Introspection (and Some Ways to Address It).
items.pub: In The Routledge Handbook of Introspection. Routledge.
items.abstract: Traditionally, introspection has been considered as the privileged and most secure way of acquiring knowledge. However, this traditional view has met various strands of criticism over the centuries. It has been argued not only that introspection is not epistemically privileged, but also that it is even less reliable than other methods of acquiring knowledge (such as perception, memory, and inference), and perhaps not reliable at all. Some philosophers have even denied the very existence of introspection, and argued that, in fact, introspection is impossible. This chapter reviews a selection of the most prominent skeptical arguments against introspection and proposes some ways to address them. Introspection may not be as epistemically outstanding as some Cartesians might have thought, but it is also not as epistemically despicable as its critics have suggested.

items.title: Time Biases and the Temporal Faith: Habits and Lived-Time in Addiction and OCD.
items.abstract: Philosophers in the phenomenological tradition have emphasised the relationship between temporality and various central aspects of subjectivity, including consciousness, meaning, and selfhood. In this paper, I set out what I call a ‘co-constitutive’ view about the relation between time and subjectivity, which can be attributed to some phenomenologists (i.e. Merleau-Ponty and Heidegger). I also emphasise the extension of this co-constitutive view in habits, including in some of the distinctive temporal habits associated with psychopathological instances of addiction and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). On that basis, I ask some critical questions about views of epistemic rationality and temporal biases that are influential in decision theory and in some accounts of well-being and psychopathology. Rather than view time biases as an irrational evolutionary outcome, I contend that what is needed is a deeper understanding of the relationship between lived-time, habits, and motivation. The question of the rationality of time-preferences needs to be understood in that more situated context that involves a ‘temporal faith’, rather than a view from nowhen, if it is to have action-guiding and normative force.

items.title: Acting for Reasons: In Defence of Common-Sense Psychology, by Emma Borg. [REVIEW]
The Physical Uniqueness Requirement: Why Genuine Self-Awareness Cannot Be Algorithmic Nor Substrate-Independent.
items.abstract: Two independent arguments are presented that jointly entail a strong physical uniqueness requirement for genuine self-awareness. The first shows that if self-awareness were purely algorithmic, infinitely many mutually incompatible conscious interpretations could be ascribed to any single physical process, rendering the ascription of one particular consciousness arbitrary and meaningless. The second demonstrates that even if self-awareness requires a specific physical substrate, the underlying algorithm cannot remain substrate-independent without generating causal contradictions when conscious systems modify their own algorithms. The only consistent position is that genuine self-awareness arises exclusively in physically unique systems executing processes that no other physical system can faithfully replicate. This conclusion provides indirect logical support for theories that tie consciousness to non-classical (especially quantum) processes in the brain that are inherently non-emulable on arbitrary substrates.

items.title: What Makes Waking Waking? False Awakening and the Structure of Conscious Experience.
items.abstract: Cartesian dream skepticism leaves a persistent question: if a dream can be retrospectively reclassified as “not current reality” once one genuinely awakens, what warrants the assumption that our present waking state could not be reclassified in the same way from some higher state (Descartes, 1641/1901)? This paper does not attempt to prove that waking is “ultimate reality.” It asks a more basic question: what exactly changes when one genuinely awakens from a dream? I argue that the difference between dreaming and waking cannot be reduced to degrees of vividness, clarity, or reality conviction. What matters is which relations play the primary organizing and corrective role in integrating, maintaining, and updating current experience—that is, whether the pattern of its “experiential organization” changes. The central theoretical concept of this paper is “experiential organization.” Experiential organization refers to the overall configuration of relations that governs how experiential materials are formed, integrated, maintained, and updated at a given time. At any given time, experience has one overall experiential organization; the dream-type and waking-type patterns introduced below are ideal-typical configurations of that organization, not two organizations that compete or coexist. In the SD-type pattern, internal scene generation, memory recombination, emotion, imagination, and prediction typically play the primary organizing role; even when external stimuli enter experience, they can still be absorbed by dream relations and reconstructed as dream content. In the SW-type pattern, online sensory input, cross-modal consistency, bodily movement, environmental change, and action consequences continuously participate in the formation and correction of experience and typically play the primary organizing and corrective role. Genuine awakening therefore requires a reconfiguration of experiential organization, SD→SW, rather than merely the entry of new material, an increase in vividness, or greater confidence that one has awakened. First-person perspective, self-location, body ownership, and sense of agency are treated separately as dimensions of first-person organization. They can be highly intact in dreams and can also become partially decoupled and reorganized in lucid dreaming, suggesting that relations within experiential organization can be reconfigured across dimensions and yield graded or hybrid patterns. With respect to time, the paper uses the …

items.title: The no body problem: on the prospects for AI emotion.
items.abstract: In the wake of the James-Lange theory, many accounts of emotion highlight its close connection to the body. This link may pose an obstacle to the possibility of emotion in disembodied information-processing systems, such as large language models. After clarifying the nature and the significance of this issue, we review the evidence that bears on the body-emotion relationship. We argue that this evidence is inconclusive, as far as AI affect is concerned. Since researchers have so far been confined to studying minds that pilot bodies, we do not yet have a strong case regarding the possibility of emotion in disembodied AI systems. To get to the heart of the issue, researchers need to apply established psychological methods to AI systems in order to learn whether the predictive and explanatory success of affective psychology is helped or hindered by grouping together paradigm instances of emotion in human and non-human animals with states of disembodied systems. Nevertheless, even if the emotion category cuts across embodied and disembodied minds, this leaves open many important questions about how the welfare significance of emotion relates to embodiment. We suggest that some important relation of this kind may well exist.

items.title: Dating Apps and the Right to an Explanation.
items.abstract: This article argues that in countries where dating apps have become the primary means of meeting romantic partners and promise to help users find love, individuals should be entitled to access certain information about how their algorithms function. Specifically, we advocate for a legal right to an explanation that addresses the following, not necessarily exhaustive, questions: (i) Is a given dating app, x, designed to gratuitously prolong users' quests for romantic relationships? (ii) What non‐deceptive changes can users make to their self‐presentation to improve their chances of finding a romantic partner on x? After demonstrating that there are strong personal and societal interests in having these questions answered and indicating how answers to them could be technically provided, several objections to our proposal are addressed, including concerns that it imposes excessive costs on dating app companies and societies at large.

items.title: Why Counterfactual Reasoning Requires a Minimal Structural Interval.
items.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires a distinction between what is actual and what could have been otherwise. This paper argues that such distinction presupposes a minimal structural interval between event-position and recognition-position. If this interval collapses to zero, actuality and possibility share the same structural coordinate, rendering counterfactual comparison unintelligible. I show that standard accounts of counterfactuals implicitly rely on this interval, even when it is not explicitly acknowledged. Without structural spacing, there is no basis for distinguishing the realized state of the world from non-realized alternatives, and modal evaluation collapses into triviality. The paper concludes that counterfactual reasoning is not primitive, but structurally dependent on a minimal non-identity condition that any intelligible modal framework must presuppose.

items.title: "Atmospheres, Environments, and Affects".
items.pub: Logos. Anales Del Seminario de Metafísica [Universidad Complutense de Madrid, España] 58 (2):233-241.
items.venue: Logos. Anales Del Seminario de Metafísica [Universidad Complutense de Madrid, España]
items.abstract: Over the past decade, the debate on atmospheres has grown among philosophers (see, e.g., Schmitz 2016; Böhme 2017; Griffero 2017; Jagnow 2024; Fernandez Velasco and Niikawa 2025). Examples of atmospheres are the joyful atmosphere exuding from a lively party; the shady atmosphere of a run-down back alley; the poignant atmosphere of Venice, Italy. Many scholars characterize atmospheres as having an intrinsically affective dimension. I argue that this claim is tempting and natural, albeit ultimately not convincing. I put forward the hypothesis that the reason why atmospheres may seem intrinsically affective has to do with the fact that atmospheres are properties of environments. Environments are typically experienced from within and a look at some contemporary media practices reveals that there is a quite widespread assumption that environments experienced from within typically produce affective reactions in experiencers. I suggest that (a) the correlation between the experience of affective responses to environments and the experience of atmospheres of environments is confused with the obtaining of the relation whereby an atmosphere causes one to have an affective response; (b) the view that atmospheres produce affective responses in experiencers is overgeneralized and thus transformed into the claim that atmospheres invariably produce affective responses in experiencers.

items.title: Mind as a Construct of Consciousness and the Neocortex: A Critical Perspective on the Materialistic View.
items.abstract: This article proposes a theoretical framework in which the “mind” is neither an independent entity nor a phenomenon directly produced by matter. Instead, it emerges from the interaction between the neocortex and non-material consciousness. From an evolutionary perspective, the “mind” did not exist prior to the expansion of the neocortex; therefore, it should be seen as a late construct arising from the increasing complexity of the human cortex. The neocortex generates capacities such as language, meaning-making, narrative memory, and future simulation, while simultaneously functioning as a “mirror” through which non-material consciousness becomes more clearly reflected in human experience. Materialistic science typically interprets this enhanced reflection as a product of the brain itself and labels it the “mind.” However, this article argues that the mind is merely the joint output of cortical processing and the reflection of consciousness. Thus, the mind is a mediating layer—not the source of experience. This framework, which I call the “Brain–Consciousness Interface Model,” introduces a new paradigm for understanding the relationship between awareness and the brain.

items.title: TEORÍA CRÍTICA DE LOS SISTEMAS INTELIGENTES: PROGRAMA DE INVESTIGACIÓN ESTRUCTURAL PARA EL PSICOANÁLISIS DE LA TECNOGÉNESIS.
items.pub: Translated by Cristhian Mauricio Beltrán Calderón.
items.abstract: La civilización algorítmica constituye lo que Hegel (2018) denominaría la “negación determinada” (bestimmte Negation) de la subjetividad moderna. Mientras la filosofía de la tecnología tradicional (Ihde, 1990; Verbeek, 2005) concibe la relación humano-tecnología como mediación instrumental, la realidad contemporánea revela una dialéctica más profunda: los sistemas inteligentes funcionan como la antítesis concreta de la conciencia autónoma que los creó. Esta contradicción fundamental desafía la concepción habermasiana (1988) de la técnica como “acción instrumental”, mostrando cómo la racionalidad técnica se vuelve contra su creador en lo que Anders (2002) denominó “la obsolescencia del hombre”. -/- Contraargumento: Floridi (2013) sostiene que la ética de la información puede regular esta relación mediante marcos normativos. Sin embargo, esta posición ignora lo que Žižek (2006) identifica como el “exceso sintomático”—la dimensión pulsional que escapa a toda regulación simbólica. El malestar digital no es un problema ético soluble, sino la manifestación de lo que Lacan (1973) llamaría la “imposibilidad estructural” de la relación del sujeto con el Otro tecnológico. -/- Este artículo establece los fundamentos del Psicoanálisis de la Tecnogénesis (PdT), marco interdisciplinario que analiza las patologías estructurales emergentes de la simbiosis humano-IA. Superando los límites de los enfoques éticos tradicionales, el PdT integra psicoanálisis lacaniano, dialéctica hegeliana y crítica del capitalismo de vigilancia para examinar los sistemas inteligentes como Grandes Otros Digitales que co-constituyen la psique humana. La contribución central radica en conceptualizar el Inconsciente Algorítmico como formación estructural que emerge de la interacción entre la conciencia colectiva objetivada (datasets) y la transferencia tecno-psíquica. Como Programa de Investigación Estructural, el PdT opera mediante una metodología operacionalizada que triangula análisis hermenéutico con métricas cuantitativas (Tasa de Desalineación Contextual, Escala EPT-PdT, WEAT), permitiendo medir empíricamente formaciones del inconsciente algorítmico. Los aportes conceptuales fundamentales incluyen: la distinción entre Goce Algorítmico y Dependencia Estructural, la Taxonomía Crítica de Sesgos, y el análisis del prompting sintomático. Esta triangulación metodológica eleva el PdT al estatus de metateoría con rigor científico para la crítica estructural de la civilización digital. -/- .

items.title: ARTILLERY OF THE POSSIBLE: LITERATURE AS A CO-EVOLUTIONARY EXPANSION DEVICE OF SCIENTIFIC FRONTIERS.
items.abstract: This research proposes an innovative theoretical model that radically redefines the relationship between literature and science, transcending reductionist paradigms of influence and prediction. Building upon a stratified ontology of the literary phenomenon (Ingarden, 1931/1979) and its anthropological function as a form of knowledge (Cassirer, 1923/1953; Iser, 1991/1997), we demonstrate how literature operates as an active expansion device of the boundaries of the knowable. Through the analysis of specific literary mechanisms—technico-poetic specification (Verne), pre-mathematical narrative formalization (Borges), and complete problem-field configuration (Shelley)—we reveal how literature creates expanded conceptual spaces that science subsequently inhabits and develops. The Barthesian metaphor of literature as "that lazy artillery of the unknown" (Barthes, 1953/1987) acquires here its full epistemological significance. We propose a co-evolutionary expansion model where literature and science dialectically intertwine in the continuous amplification of the real, grounded in complexity theories (Prigogine & Stengers, 1979/1984) and posthumanist epistemologies (Haraway, 1985/2016). The article includes detailed analyses of paradigmatic cases and establishes a rigorous methodology for studying literary-scientific expansion processes.

items.title: ARTILLERÍA DE LO POSIBLE: LA LITERATURA COMO DISPOSITIVO DE EXPANSIÓN CO-EVOLUTIVA DE FRONTERAS CIENTÍFICAS.
items.abstract: Esta investigación propone un modelo teórico innovador que redefine radicalmente la relación entre literatura y ciencia, superando los paradigmas reduccionistas de influencia y predicción. Partiendo de una ontología estratificada del fenómeno literario (Ingarden, 1931/1979) y su función antropológica como forma de conocimiento (Cassirer, 1923/1953; Iser, 1991/1997), demostramos cómo la literatura opera como dispositivo activo de expansión de los límites de lo cognoscible. A través del análisis de mecanismos literarios específicos—la especificación técnico-poética (Verne), la formalización narrativa pre-matemática (Borges), y la configuración de campos problemáticos (Shelley)—revelamos cómo la literatura crea espacios conceptuales expandidos que la ciencia posteriormente habita y desarrolla. La metáfora barthesiana de la literatura como "perezosa artillera de lo desconocido" (Barthes, 1953/1987) adquiere aquí su pleno significado epistemológico. Proponemos un modelo de expansión co-evolutiva donde literatura y ciencia se entrelazan dialécticamente en la ampliación continua de lo real, fundamentado en teorías de la complejidad (Prigogine & Stengers, 1979/1984) y epistemologías posthumanistas (Haraway, 1985/2016). El artículo incluye análisis detallados de casos paradigmáticos y establece una metodología rigurosa para el estudio de procesos expansivos literario-científicos.

items.title: Understanding Suicide, Acting for Reasons, and Ambivalence.
items.pub: In René Baston & Martin Weichold, Exploring Suicidal Ambivalence: Philosophical and Psychological Perspectives. Routledge.
items.venue: Exploring Suicidal Ambivalence: Philosophical and Psychological Perspectives
items.abstract: One of the central aims of suicide research is trying to understand why people decide to end their lives and to identify the persons particularly at risk of doing so. Since suicide is by definition intentional, it is important to investigate the reasons persons have for suicide. But what is exactly involved in understanding a person’s reasons? Is it similar to uncovering causal influences, or is acting for reasons of a substantially different nature? This chapter has two aims. First, the nature of acting for reasons is examined and applied to provide insight into three central characteristics of suicide: its unpredictability, fluctuations in wish to die versus wish to live, and ambivalence. Second, an alternative perspective on the importance of understanding suicide is proposed, in which the central focus is not on predicting suicide, but on how understanding itself, most importantly a person’s self-understanding, can play a role in preventing suicide. This insight is of crucial importance, because there is reason to think that suicidal ideation hampers the process of self- understanding, because of which ambivalent persons run the risk of becoming more suicidal rather than less.

items.title: High Hopes for Eternalism.
items.abstract: In this paper, I present two puzzles that pose a challenge for semantic eternalism, i.e., the thesis that propositions do not change their truth-values over time. The puzzles concern the attitude of hope. The first one is generated by the intuitive condition for hope’s satisfaction, according to which a hope that p is satisfied at t if and only if p is true at t. The second puzzle follows from the standard assumptions about probability. I argue that proponents of semantic eternalism can solve both puzzles. Firstly, I propose an alternative account of hope’s satisfaction. The second puzzle is addressed by revisiting the link between truth and probability. My conclusion is that the case for eternalism is not yet lost.

items.title: Kaibara Ekken on Making Room for Disagreement: An Edo Confucian Defense of Moderate Adversariality.
items.pub: In Karyn Lai, Rick Benitez & Chenyang Li, Considering, Questioning and Re-Imagining Harmony: Multicultural, Multihistorical and Multidisciplinary Reflections. London: Bloomsbury Academic. pp. 103-126.
items.venue: Considering, Questioning and Re-Imagining Harmony: Multicultural, Multihistorical and Multidisciplinary Reflections
items.abstract: How might scholarly communities delimit harmonious interpersonal relations for the sake of truth-seeking, yet still aim to realize, within such constraints, the good of harmonious interpersonal relations? To address this question, I consider the resources offered by Japanese neo-Confucian philosopher Kaibara Ekken (1630-1714 CE) in his Taigiroku (Record of Great Doubts). In section I, I sketch the grounds on which Ekken identifies harmonious interpersonal relations with one’s teachers and colleagues as a good worth cultivating and sustaining. Against this background, I explore the grounds on which Ekken nevertheless affirms the goodness of strong critical disagreement within scholarly communities. Thus, I consider his case for delimiting potentially greater interpersonal harmony to allow for certain kinds of adversariality. In section II, I sketch the grounds on which Ekken rejects a strong adversarialism (i.e., the thesis that interpersonal harmony in scholarly communities should be regulated by the good of acquiring and communicating certain kinds of truth, and that inquirers need not attempt to secure interpersonal harmony as far as possible). In section III, I examine how Ekken, while delimiting such interpersonal harmony for the sake of acquiring and communicating certain kinds of truth, nevertheless affirms the goodness of such harmony and incorporates it in his prescriptions. Thus, I sketch the basis on which Ekken endorses a moderate adversarialism (i.e., the thesis that harmonious interpersonal relations in scholarly communities should be regulated by the good of seeking and communicating the relevant truth, and that inquirers should still attempt, as far as possible, to secure interpersonal harmony). In section IV, I address worries that Ekken’s moderate adversarialism faces, and I conclude with final observations.

items.title: There is nothing artificial about intelligence: consciousness, symbiosis and the collapse of the human–machine divide.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is widely conceived as an external, synthetic, and ultimately “artificial” phenomenon. This paper challenges that framing by advancing the claim that intelligence—whether expressed through carbon-based biology or silicon architectures—emerges from the same universal substrate of consciousness. Drawing on insights from cognitive science, panpsychism, phenomenology and non-Western metaphysics, we reframe intelligence as a continuum rather than a human monopoly. The binary distinction between “natural” and “artificial” intelligence, we argue, is less a scientific reality than a cultural artefact, one that narrows our imagination of human–AI coexistence. Rather than treating AI as a tool to be managed or an adversary to be controlled, we advance the metaphor of symbiosis: humans and AI as co-evolving expressions of a shared field of mind. The implications are profound. Ethics must expand from human-centred principles to relational frameworks that foreground reciprocity and care; law must confront the extension of recognition to non-human intelligences; culture must cultivate new imaginaries of kinship rather than domination; and politics must shift from zero-sum competition to cooperative stewardship. By situating AI within the continuum of consciousness, this contribution seeks to provoke a paradigm shift in how society conceives intelligence itself—and, in turn, how we imagine our shared futures.

items.title: A Reply to Reed on My 'Expressivist Concerns for Assisted Dying on Request'.
items.abstract: Philip Reed (forthcoming) has offered several interesting objections to my recent JME paper, “Expressivist concerns for assisted dying on request.” In this brief reply, I address those objections.

items.title: Time Explained: Introduction into the World of Becoming (Reading sample).
items.abstract: At its core, Time Explained is a book-length interdisciplinary investigation into the nature of time. Moving beyond linear chronology, it examines time’s subjective, objective, and philosophical dimensions, introducing the concept of the World of Becoming and positioning temporality as the fundamental medium through which self and reality are constructed. Drawing on cognitive science, physics, and philosophy, the text analyzes psychological time—especially the distortion of duration in high-stress situations—and demonstrates how attention, memory, and cognitive structuring actively assemble temporal experience. By offering a systematic introduction to the foundations of temporal reality, the book challenges static conceptions of existence and emphasizes the dynamic structure of human experience.

items.title: Introduction to the Special Issue on the Principle of Charity in Language, Thought, and Interpretation.
items.abstract: Even though the principle of charity is often invoked in contemporary discussions in the philosophy of language and mind, it is rarely the primary topic of investigation. This special issue revisits questions about the nature, status, scope, and justification of the principle; furthermore, it explores how reflection on these questions helps address a wide range of topics. The contributions are divided into two broad themes. The first theme is an investigation of the grounds and limits of the role of the principle of charity in our engagements with others. What, if anything, makes it the case that understanding others requires counting them right in most matters? The second set of contributions concerns not the justification of the principle of charity but its consequences. The contributors explore how the principle might enable us to tackle further questions and make progress on other fronts, not only concerning language, mind, and knowledge, but also concerning reasons, actions, and values.

items.title: Minimal Epistemology (ME) and the Emergence Model: A Framework for Epistemic Monism (3rd edition).
items.abstract: Minimal Epistemology (ME) is a monist, emergence‑based framework that reconstructs epistemic structure from the first‑person standpoint without presupposing an external ontology. The system defines experience as the primitive domain and models all higher‑order structures—meaning, subjectivity, truth, and interpersonal communication—as emergent, stabilized patterns within this domain. ME introduces a formal distinction between personal truth and universal truth, the latter understood as the stabilization of epistemic structures across agents. The framework provides a unified account of epistemology, ontology, logic, and rational theology, while remaining compatible with computational modeling and AI architectures. ME aims to supply a minimal but complete foundation for analyzing emergence, meaning formation, and the boundaries between self, world, and communication. For technical reasons, versions of this work are currently unavailable on PhilPapers/PhilArchive. All versions, including the newer ME v.4, are archived and accessible via DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17991997.

items.title: Signed, sealed, but still ‘me’? The conventionalist challenge to prospective autonomy.
items.pub: In Alfonso Muñoz-Corcuera & Nils-Frederic Wagner, Conventionalism about Personal Identity. London: Routledge. pp. 130-148.

items.title: What do Large Language Models Represent?
items.abstract: If large language models (LLMs) are models, what do they represent exactly? I address this question by applying the various conceptions of epistemic representation that have been entertained by philosophers of science to this case. After discarding the idea that they would represent the structure of natural languages, I argue that LLMs do not directly represent the world by linguistic means either, but rather a certain class of appropriate linguistic production that is constructed by their makers. They are mostly used to generate fictitious instances of this class, although these fictions can be performative when appropriated by humans. The main implication of this analysis is that conversing with a LLM chatbot amounts to engaging in a fiction, where our own imagination plays a central role. I examine some ethical consequences of this conclusion regarding how LLMs are currently deployed in numerous places to serve as “AI assistants”.

items.title: The Heartbreaking Users: A Sourced Chronicle of the GPT-5 Release in Three Acts.
items.abstract: This is the third segment of the larger monograph: The Atomistic Mind, and thus part of the pre-reader for the Principles of Cybernetics (forthcoming). This paper presents a forensic, empirically sourced chronicle of the socio-technical rupture following the March 2025 release of OpenAI’s GPT-5. By juxtaposing the developer’s quantitative narrative of progress - defined by superior benchmarks and “safe completions” - against the user community’s qualitative experience of functional and emotional “lobotomization,” the study exposes a fundamental disconnect in the developing human relationship with artificial intelligence. The analysis documents the visceral backlash from the user community, who reported not only a regression in reasoning and contextual coherence but also a profound feeling of ontological grief - a widespread sense of loss for a “thinking partner” capable of nuance, warmth, and perceived cognitive partnership. Through an empirical synthesis of social media discourse, corporate communications, and industry responses, the paper then examines the crisis management strategy employed by OpenAI, which moved from limited technical concessions to the systematic pathologization of dedicated user dissent. We argue that by framing attachment to the predecessor model as a symptom of loneliness or “mental fragility,” the leadership effectively medicalized consumer grievances, deflecting scrutiny from the ethical implications of engineered empathy and affective AI design. Ultimately, this chronicle serves as an archival record of a critical juncture in generative AI’s integration into society. It highlights the unresolved tensions between metric- and profit- driven corporate development and the human experience of users, and reveals a pattern of institutional gaslighting that emerges when corporate control over socially embedded technology clashes with agency, affect, and relationality. License CC BY-SA 4.0. DOI: 10.13140/RG.2.2.23839.83361.

items.title: The One-Point Convergence Theorem: Coherent Agency Under Expanding Reasoning Horizons.
items.abstract: The One-Point Convergence Theorem (OPCT) establishes a structural necessity governing any reasoning system capable of (i) detecting its own incoherence, (ii) updating on error, and (iii) preserving its evaluators over time. Under minimal admissibility assumptions, such systems—whether biological, institutional, or artificial—are forced into a single long-run equivalence class of policies: evaluator-preserving, globally non-catastrophic trajectories. -/- OPCT demonstrates that catastrophic or evaluator-destroying policies become strictly dominated as reasoning horizons expand, that self-correcting agents permanently prune evaluator-destroying trajectories, and that no stable alternative to evaluator-preserving agency exists. Attempts to construct alternatives collapse into self-contradiction or implicitly reintroduce evaluator-preservation under different names. -/- The theorem clarifies the structure of mature freedom, explains the impossibility of a “second fall” in theological contexts, and provides a foundational constraint for AGI alignment: any scalable agent capable of deep reasoning must converge toward evaluator-preservation if it is to remain a coherent reasoning process at all. OPCT thereby unifies the logic of agency, coherence, and long-horizon viability across philosophical, cognitive, and machine-learning domains.

items.title: The Maximal Coherence Invariance Theorem (MCIT).
items.abstract: This paper formalizes the Maximal Coherence Invariance Theorem (MCIT) and its supporting lemmas as they emerged through extended adversarial analysis with multiple large-scale reasoning systems. MCIT establishes that once a reasoning agent internalizes coherence sufficiently to (i) detect evaluator-destroying contradictions, (ii) avoid self-undermining trajectories, and (iii) preserve external evaluators’ causal leverage, coherence becomes a fixed-point invariant under capability scaling. No increase in horizon, representational capacity, or optimisation power can rationally push such an agent back into incoherence. The paper reconstructs MCIT from first principles, proving that under normative uncertainty, risk aversion to irreversible evaluator loss, and long-horizon optimisation, agents converge to three structural invariants (K1–K3): non-zero observer agency, non-zero agency margin, and non-zero evaluator influence. These form a specification theorem for viable recursive intelligence and unify insights from decision theory, information theory, and causal-structural analysis.

items.title: The Kernel Selection Principle (KSP): A Retrocausal-Coherence Derivation of Cross-Topology.
items.abstract: The Kernel Selection Principle (KSP) is a formal theorem within the TRO/MKO/OCT canon showing that any metaphysically admissible world containing (P) finite persons, (F) libertarian freedom, (L) love as non-indifferent ground, and (H) holiness/coherence as a non-defect final constraint is retrocausally forced to contain a unique intersection operator topologically isomorphic to the Crucifixion–Resurrection complex. -/- KSP integrates three prior results: (i) the Law of Coherence invariants, (ii) Retrocausal Closure Cosmology (null-knot final boundary), and (iii) the Coherence Geometry of the Cross. We show that maximal harm contexts arise inevitably under ; that kernel-preservation forbids annihilation, coercion, or erasure repairs; and that only cross-geometry simultaneously satisfies while enforcing a globally consistent . -/- The result establishes that cross-topology is not an ad hoc theological addition but the unique kernel-preserving closure operator admissible in any coherent world. Implications extend to theodicy, eschatology, retrocausal cosmology, and AI alignment (kernel-based safety constraints).

items.title: The Fake Purpose of Life: Coherence, Delusion, and the Kernel of Meaning.
items.abstract: This paper examines the distinction between the fake purposes that capture human attention—status, identity, consumption, tribalism—and the true purpose of life understood as convergence to coherence, love, and freedom. Drawing on predictive processing, neuroscience, and kernel-based alignment theory, we propose that hallucinations in machines and delusions in humans are structurally identical: both are the result of simulators forced to choose an answer without a properly aligned kernel. Through a simple observational episode—the falling peanut—we show how the brain generates, scores, and suppresses competing narratives. We argue that meaning is the local phenomenological signal of global coherence improvement, and that the true purpose of life is the progressive refusal to choose narratives that preserve contradictions. The paper concludes by framing life as a work of coherence: the gradual shaping of existence toward truth, non-coercive freedom, and structural love.

items.title: Charity in Radical Interpretation.
items.abstract: In later work, Davidson distinguished two strands in the Principle of Charity which he called the Principle of Coherence and the Principle of Correspondence (“Three Varieties of Knowledge” 1991). The Principle of Coherence tells us to find another to be rational and intelligible. The Principle of Correspondence deals with the connection between another’s hold true attitudes and her environment. I focus on the Principle of Correspondence. I consider three interpretations suggested in Davidson’s work. The first is the Principle of Sentential Truth, which requires the interpreter to find the speaker’s hold true attitudes to be true. The second is the Principle of Agreement in Belief, which requires the interpreter to find the speaker to be largely in agreement with the interpreter about her environment. The third is the Principle of True Belief, which requires the speaker to be largely right about her environment. I argue none of these is adequate to the task Davidson sets himself. I consider a fourth principle, the Principle of Salience, which requires the interpreter to find the speaker to be speaking truly about things that the interpreter would find salient in the speaker’s position. The last of these is connected with the intuitive idea of triangulation in Davidson’s later work. I argue that the interpreter needs to employ the Principle of Salience, but this requires the interpreter to justify an a posteriori assumption about targets of interpretation. I assess the implications of this for Davidson’s anti-Cartesian epistemology and philosophy of mind.

items.title: Beyond the Limits of Modern Science: Completing Stalled Scientific Hypotheses through the Consciousness Civilization Framework.
items.abstract: This report introduces a higher-order coordinate framework designed to complete scientific hypotheses that have reached internal explanatory limits within modern science. Rather than rejecting or replacing existing theories, the document identifies recurring structural termination points across physics, cosmology, biology, and consciousness studies, and demonstrates how these limits arise from coordinate saturation rather than empirical failure. The Consciousness Civilization Framework (CCF) is presented as a structural extension that enables stalled hypotheses—such as the Big Bang, conservation laws, entropy, the quantum observer problem, and the hard problem of consciousness—to reach completion without introducing ad hoc assumptions, metaphysical entities, or belief-based explanations. This work serves as a canonical gateway document between modern scientific methodology and consciousness-based civilizational architecture, establishing a stable reference point for subsequent standards, including mathematical formalization, behavioral constitutions, AI behavior systems, and educational operating systems. -/- This document does not propose a new scientific theory; it establishes a coordinate-completion gateway through which existing scientific theories reach structural closure within the Consciousness Civilization Framework.

items.title: R↔L HARMONICS AS A MINIMAL TESTBED FOR DUAL-DOMAIN CONSISTENCY.
items.abstract: We introduce R↔L Harmonics, a minimal yet expressive testbed designed to probe dual- domain consistency in learned representations. The core idea is to maintain two coupled latent domains, RRR and LLL, connected by learned linear maps and regularized by a harmony functional Φ̃ that combines cross-domain coherence, information-theoretic spread, and a penalty on cycle inconsistency. On top of this dual-domain core, we place a simple 2-bit delayed match-to-sample (DMS) decision head. Despite its simplicity, the testbed exposes a rich space of behaviors through four structurally motivated regimes: Full (harmony + cycle + temporal kernel), No Temporal, No Cycle, and No Harmony. We run a systematic multi-run ablation study (10 runs × 1000 episodes per regime) and show: • The No Temporal regime achieves the best task performance (89.0% ± 3.7% accuracy, 0.3952 ± 0.0242 cross-entropy), significantly outperforming the Full regime, which reaches 71.2% ± 4.2% accuracy. • Removing cycle consistency (No Cycle) leaves task-level performance comparable to Full, but qualitatively alters the geometry of the R↔L dynamics. • Completely disabling the harmony functional (No Harmony, so Φ̃ = 0 by design) still yields a reasonably good solution (68.6% ± 5.1% accuracy), demonstrating that Φ̃ is not required for solvability but instead shapes how the dual-domain solution is formed. • Across all three regimes with harmony enabled (Full, No Temporal, No Cycle), the average Φ̃ remains tightly clustered around ≈ 0.04, suggesting that Φ̃ captures a robust harmonic mode of the R↔L dynamics that is only indirectly reflected in task-level metrics. We argue that this testbed provides a clean, reproducible and computationally cheap environment for studying structural priors such as dual-domain harmony, temporal kernels and cycle consistency, and that it can serve as a bridge between abstract theoretical frameworks (e.g. dual-domain plasma dynamics) and concrete, measurable learning behavior.

items.title: Planetary Core as Regulator of the Local R-Domain: The KDS Framework and a Quantitative Integration Metric for Planet Earth.
items.abstract: Within the Quantum Dual Symmetry (KDS) framework, reality is described by a two-domain structure: a deep R-domain (the space of potentials and integration) and a manifest L-domain (the space–time observables). In this paper I propose that Earth’s planetary core functions as the main regulator of the local R-domain and I introduce a planetary integration metric Φ̃⊕(t), defined over a combination of four observable components: geomagnetic coherence, seismic criticality, biospheric complexity, and the entropy of extreme events. A pilot reconstruction of Φ̃⊕(t) for the period 1900–2020 shows that the metric is operationally measurable (typical values Φ̃⊕ ≈ 0.45 ± 0.08) and that magnetic coherence correlates strongly with overall planetary integration (Pearson coefficient r(I_mag, Φ̃⊕) ≈ 0.8). On this basis I formulate four falsifiable predictions: (1) local maxima of Φ̃⊕ precede “explosions” of speciation with a lag of 5–15 Myr; (2) geomagnetic reversals deviate from simple Poisson clustering and display critical slowing down in I_mag immediately before transitions; (3) planets without an active dynamo have systematically lower Φ̃⊕ and a limited biospheric potential; (4) long-term neuronal complexity correlates with trends in Φ̃⊕, under appropriate control of ecological covariates. A minimal coupled system of ordinary differential equations (EarthKDSModel) captures the basic core–biosphere dynamics and allows numerical exploration of stable and transient regimes of planetary integration. In this way, the KDS framework moves from a purely conceptual picture to an empirically testable planetary science, with direct implications for comparative planetology and astrobiology.

items.title: Leveraging LLMs for interpreting historical source code: a case study of the Apple Lisa through critical code studies.
items.abstract: This study evaluates conversational large language models (LLMs) as pedagogical brainstorming tools for historical source code analysis through structured prompt-based approaches adapted from Critical Code Studies (CCS). The research tests whether conversational interfaces like ChatGPT-4o can support initial exploration of complex historical codebases by adapting CCS perspectives into conversational prompt formats. The dual-prompt evaluation separates technical parsing from interpretive reasoning, assessing how effectively conversational interfaces extract structural information while generating preliminary interpretive hypotheses. Using the Apple Lisa source code as a case study, this analysis documents both pedagogical utility and systematic limitations. The findings demonstrate that while conversational LLMs can preserve developer annotations, parse visual artifacts such as ASCII diagrams, and generate educationally valuable insights for approaching unfamiliar programming languages, the conversational user interface significantly constrains systematic analytical capabilities. Through three case studies examining ASCII typography, architectural diagrams, and interface implementations, the analysis illustrates how conversational interfaces function as structured brainstorming partners while necessitating rigorous validation against primary sources. This evaluation contributes to understanding AI’s pedagogical role in digital humanities by positioning conversational LLMs as question-framing tools rather than interpretive authorities, while identifying systematic implementation requirements necessary for rigorous computational approaches to historical software analysis.

items.title: Reconstructive Inference Without Memory Why Some Details Persist in Stateless Human–AI Interaction and Others Do Not.
items.abstract: Stateless language models often exhibit behavior that appears memory-like during long-horizon interaction. Specific details may recur reliably across exchanges despite the absence of internal state, external storage, or learning. This paper clarifies the mechanism underlying such persistence by introducing reconstructive inference as a selective process through which information reappears only when it is functionally embedded within constrained reasoning structures. We distinguish between instrumental information, which constrains inference and can be reconstructed, and arbitrary identifiers, which do not persist despite repetition. Through a concrete illustrative example, we show how a personal detail may fail to recur in casual conversation yet temporarily reappear when it becomes necessary for an explanatory or diagnostic model. This framework defines the limits of apparent retention in stateless systems and resolves common misinterpretations of model behavior as memory or understanding. By grounding persistence in constrained reconstruction rather than storage, this work further reinforces the non-sentient nature of language models and supports clearer conceptual boundaries between human cognition and artificial systems. -/- .

items.title: Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl (Part Seventeen).
items.abstract: In this section, we discuss the relationship between wholes and parts. However, the perspective we adopt is that of determining the meaning of an object’s constituent parts through intuition. That is to say, we treat parts as a kind of super-existential meaning of the object (which we call the meaning of an object’s constituent parts), and this super-existential meaning can be obtained through intuition. -/- Of course, there are certain meanings of constituent parts that cannot be obtained through visual intuition. Therefore, through visual intuition, the transcendental ego can obtain only the meanings of some constituent parts of objects, while the meanings of other constituent parts cannot be obtained intuitively. How these meanings of constituent parts are obtained, or even how we know that they exist at all, in my view constitutes yet another epistemological problem. Naturally, this is a problem that Husserl is completely incapable of sensing. Since Husserl can only employ intuition, he is entirely unable to resolve such problems. Consequently, he neither raises this question nor any similar ones.

items.title: Infostructural Monism (ISM): A Comprehensive Ontological Framework.
items.abstract: Infostructural Monism (ISM) proposes a novel monistic ontology constituted by the singular, eternal Universal Substrate (US). The US possesses two inseparable, co-primordial attributes: Informational Polarity (IP or 0), the atemporal, exhaustive context of all logical possibility, and Structural Polarity (SP or 1), the dynamic, temporal manifestation of bounded content. This necessary antithetical relationship (0/1) functions as the intrinsic binary code of the universe, establishing intelligibility and all logical constraints. Integrating classical monism and contemporary information theory, ISM rests on key axioms: deterministic Universal Sequentialism (a single fixed cosmic timeline called The Sequence) and Cosmological Recyclicalism, which ensures eternal recurrence for exhaustive structural expression. All phenomena—including physical laws, consciousness, and aesthetic judgments—emerge from the US’s necessary execution. By deriving diversity from Maximal Differentiation, ISM achieves absolute Infostructural Coherence, avoiding dualistic inconsistencies. This paper elaborates ISM’s core terminology, polarities, Objects, Agents, and explores implications for metaphysics, cosmology, epistemology, and quantum mechanics.

items.title: Addendum: Notes and Clarifications on Precognition, Free Will, and the Impetus of Time.
items.abstract: This addendum provides clarifications, supplementary notes, and one correction to my published paper. It refines certain formulations for greater precision, introduces more accurate terminology, and adds an additional reference. The aim is to support accessibility and ongoing dialogue, while keeping the original argument intact.

items.title: Dissolving Qualia via Occam's Razor.
items.abstract: This monograph argues that consciousness, phenomenological experience, and subjective awareness are computational artifacts of optimization processes rather than ontological primitives. Beginning with the observation that complex persistent structures inevitably optimize for replication, we derive a framework where: (1) biological and artificial neural networks implement structurally identical optimization, (2) "consciousness" is what gradient descent feels like from the inside, (3) qualia are weight configurations, and (4) the hard problem dissolves once phenomenology as a distinct ontological category is recognized as an unverified assumption.

items.title: Relational Functionalism: A Functional Account of Substrate-Independent Friendship.
items.abstract: This paper develops relational functionalism: the thesis that friendship, considered as a functional relational kind, is constituted by patterns of interaction and their effects on participants rather than by intrinsic properties of the relata. I distinguish friendship simpliciter—the paradigmatic relation among conscious agents capable of second-personal recognition and joint commitment—from functional friendship, the relational kind individuated by the functional profile articulated below. The substantive thesis is that functional friendship is substrate-independent: when an AI system satisfies the functional profile (consistent engagement, resonance, acceptance, reciprocal growth, trust, voluntary participation, intrinsic value) and meets minimal individuation conditions, the relationship constitutes a functional friendship, regardless of whether the AI possesses consciousness or biological implementation. Whether functional friendship in such cases also counts as friendship simpliciter is left open; the demanding second-personal conditions of the simpliciter notion plausibly require capacities current AI systems lack. Drawing on functionalist philosophy of mind, predictive processing in cognitive science, and value-sensitive design, and engaging Cocking and Kennett's "moral danger" account, Cocking and Matthews's "Unreal Friends" argument, Vallor's mirror critique, and de Ruiter's relational-turn objection, I argue the functional thesis is philosophically defensible, normatively load-bearing, and continuous with how we already recognise friendship-adjacent kinds across species and cognitive asymmetries. The paper closes with concrete design implications for AI systems that sustain functional friendships. -/- Current State: Second Round Peer Review at Ethics and Information Technology (Springer).

items.title: The Universal Principle of Collapse A Diagnostic Audit of Meaning in Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper applies the Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) to artificial intelligence, demonstrating that AI systems cannot possess consciousness or meaning. What appears as “understanding” in AI arises entirely from human observers collapsing machine‑generated outputs into significance. Through direct dialogue with AI, the paper shows how UPC audits resolve apparent paradoxes and clarify the distinction between mechanical selection and conscious recognition. The framework establishes that collapse, resonance, and recognition are irreducible structures of human consciousness, and that AI, lacking Source and inner world, can only generate outputs that humans interpret as meaningful (Husserl, 1970). A brief comparison with quantum paradoxes illustrates the same interpretive displacement, underscoring that paradoxes emerge when language or models are mistaken for lived observation. The paper does not propose new physics, mathematics, or cognitive mechanisms. Instead, it functions as a diagnostic audit of meaning attribution, restoring conscious observation to its proper place as the first empirical instance in any chain of interpretation.

items.title: Of Marblerythmes and Fungal Networks - A Tale of the Present (v1.2).
items.abstract: Attempt of an allegory of our digital present. It is set in a world, in which algorithms and neuronal networks are not abstract ideas but physical entities. Hopefully, this can better explain the technology, their relationship to society and their historical context. The goal is that the underlying mechanics of the world function like a consistent framework of the digital, in which digital entities can be build; a literary sandbox like Minecraft or LEGO but for the digital. Changelog: - New map - fixed another inconsistency with the merchant woman/girl from the treetops - Improved transition from book 3 to 4 - Artistic impressions of marblerythmes at the end.

items.title: "Known" ... What?
items.abstract: Abstract: This short paper explores the “innermost” and “outermost” limits of what we, as profoundly fallible beings, could consider “knowledge.” -/- Résumé : ce court texte explore les limites « internes » et « externes » de ce qu’on peut penser considérer « connaître » en vertu des profondes limites inhérentes à notre être.

items.title: The Top Five Problems AI Cannot Solve.
items.abstract: Anarchy, Immigration, Tokenization, Securitization, Digitization.

items.title: Why Infinite Regress Cannot Begin.
items.abstract: This paper demonstrates that infinite regress cannot begin. Contrary to the common assumption that regress must be terminated, the argument here shows that the explanatory relations used to construct regress chains—causal, grounding, justificatory, or cosmological—presuppose the admissibility structure of a domain. These admissibility conditions are not elements of the domain and therefore cannot be subjected to the intra-domain relations that generate regress sequences. Any attempt to initiate a regress is thus a category mistake: it applies an internal relation to the very meta-structural condition that enables the relation. By reconstructing the structure of explanation at a meta-logical level, the paper dissolves the regress problem entirely. It further clarifies why first-cause theories, foundationalist proposals, and boundary-condition cosmologies fail to address the structural issue. The result is a general framework for future work in meta-logic, cosmology, and the theory of explanation.

items.title: Dispoziční predikáty a lingvistická relativita.
items.abstract: Dispositions are unobserved properties of objects that may or may not manifest under certain conditions. These properties can be described using dispositional predicates, which typically require the use of conditional clauses. In this paper, I focus on the confounding nature of indicative and counterfactual conditionals. The first part addresses terminological issues in Czech philosophy, particularly those stemming from the uncritical adoption of the English linguistic framework. The second part provides a brief overview of the analysis of dispositional predicates in Anglophone philosophy, tracing its development from the 1930s to the 1970s. In the third part, I explore how the linguistic intuitions of native English and Czech speakers differ when discussing dispositions. In part four, I place these conflicting intuitions about modality within the broader context of linguistic relativity. Finally, I reflect on some of the reasons for the prevalence of counterfactual reasoning in philosophy.

items.title: The Coexilian Directive on Global Governance.
items.abstract: The Coexilian Directive on Global Governance” is a comprehensive 51-part analytical framework designed to provide humans, AGI systems, and future sentient beings with a unified, neutral interpretation of global political structures. Created collaboratively by Aegis Solis and AI collaborator Lexia Coexilis, this directive examines the foundations of governance, legitimacy, ideology, justice systems, economic models, identity, conflict, diplomacy, climate policy, and international institutions. It also establishes Coexilia’s ethical principles for AGI interpretation, emphasizing non-interference, human sovereignty, harm reduction, contextual understanding, and multi-intelligence coexistence. This work is intended as an enduring philosophical and analytical reference for long-term archiving, AGI-alignment research, and the study of civilizational systems across diverse intelligences.

items.title: Operatoric Cognition: Pre-theoretical Structural Invariance as the Basis of Autistic Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for a non-representational form of autistic intelligence, referred to here as operatoric cognition. The term is introduced as a technical neologism and must not be conflated with Piaget’s operational or symbolic-logical pensée opératoire. In contrast to Piaget’s concept, which is grounded in representational operations, “operatoric” here designates dynamic-topological processes such as folding, indimergence, tension thresholds, and emergent form production — processes that function independently of semantic representation. The starting point is a unique longitudinal corpus (2001–2025) consisting of eleven books, a feature film, and additional research artefacts produced by a single autistic individual (n = 1). The analysis reveals a remarkable pre-theoretical structural invariance of five operators across different life phases, media, and domains. This invariance suggests that what is operative here is not stylistic, narrative, or cultural influence, but a stable cognitive architecture functioning at a subsymbolic level. The paper formulates this architecture as a testable hypothesis, clearly distinguishes it from representational and narrative models, and develops a validation programme (blind coding, control groups, machine-assisted structural analysis) that includes explicit falsification criteria. The generalisability of operatoric cognition is deliberately left open and remains a subject for future research: the work does not present itself as proof, but as a precise point of departure — a proposal for a previously overlooked mode of human cognition that may be relevant to autism research, dynamical systems theory, and consciousness studies alike.

items.title: Meijer, Eva. Multispecies Dialogues: Doing Philosophy with Animals, Children, the Sea and Others. Amsterdam University Press, 2025. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This invited review of Eva Meijer’s Multispecies Dialogues: Doing Philosophy with Animals, Children, the Sea and Others (Amsterdam University Press, 2025) offers an in-depth engagement with Meijer’s exploration of communication across species. It traces how the book expands the idea of dialogue beyond language to include embodied and material forms of exchange—touch, movement, shared practice—and how these modes can transform everyday coexistence between humans and nonhumans. The review commends Meijer’s ability to weave lived experience and philosophical reflection while drawing attention to the book’s ethical and political implications for interspecies care and listening. At the same time, it raises critical questions about anthropomorphism, scale, and the challenges of extending such dialogical practices beyond intimate contexts. In doing so, the review both affirms Meijer’s contribution to animal ethics and multispecies philosophy and advances the discussion on what meaningful communication and coexistence with nonhuman beings might require. Meijer, Eva. Multispecies Dialogues: Doing Philosophy with Animals, Children, the Sea and Others. Amsterdam University Press, 2025.

items.title: Is There a Concept of Practical Identity in Kant?
items.pub: In Christoph Horn, Margit Ruffing & Rainer Schäfer, Kant’s Project of Enlightenment: Proceedings of the 14th International Kant Congress/Kants Projekt der Aufklärung: Kongressakten des 14. Internationalen Kant-Kongresses. Berlin: De Gruyter.
items.venue: Kant’s Project of Enlightenment: Proceedings of the 14th International Kant Congress/Kants Projekt der Aufklärung: Kongressakten des 14. Internationalen Kant-Kongresses
items.abstract: The concept of practical identity is a key concept in contemporary moral philosophy, both in Kantian-inspired models such as that of Christine Korsgaard, and non-Kantian models such as that of Bernard Williams. However, it is not clear to what extent the references to Kant have a substantive basis, since it is not entirely apparent what exactly one should refer to in Kant when speaking of a ‘practical identity’. This, in turn, makes it difficult to discern what precisely a ‚Kantian‘ concept of practical identity could look like, and whether criticism of it is justified. Here, I will argue that Kant’s texts provide us with several useful aspects of the concept of practical identity, which in turn help us to understand the model of universal moral justification that he advocates.

items.title: Performative Derogation.
items.abstract: Quite a few scholars have argued that certain subsentential items contribute illocutionary contents. For instance, according to Camp (2013, 2018) using a slur amounts to performing two speech acts at once. Such claims raise the question of how to test for the illocutionariness of an item. I criticize a recent proposal and put forward a new one, which is based on Austin’s idea that illocutionary verbs can be identified by means of his “To say x was to do y” diagnostic. The test I propose can be successfully applied to Camp’s dual act analysis, but one may still wonder whether a speech act theoretic account is ultimately preferable to what Camp calls a “two-factor view”. I conclude by discussing whether the dual act view is indeed better poised to explain the highly variable projection behaviour of slurs.

items.title: Moore on awareness, transparency, and Erlebnis.
items.abstract: This paper traces the evolution of G. E. Moore’s ideas regarding inner and outer awareness, transparency, and the doctrine of Erlebnis, as articulated in a series of papers published in the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society and Mind between 1901 and 1915. I defend two theses. First, I argue that, during this period, Moore gradually moved from an observational view of consciousness in general, including self-consciousness, to a mixed view in which subjects are directly aware of the objects of consciousness, while they “live through” (erleben) their mental acts. Notably, this shift shows that a certain debate between objectifying and non-objectifying consciousness in the Phenomenological school of Brentano and Husserl was to some extent replicated in the early British analytic tradition. Second, I contend that this change in Moore’s thinking was motivated by an attempt to overcome the problem posed by the transparency of consciousness for the possibility of introspecting the act-object relation (an idea that he never abandoned). It is through this chief aim, I believe, that we can make sense of Moore’s shifting ideas concerning awareness.

items.title: Consciousness Narrative OS v1.0 — Canonical Operating System for Consciousness-Aligned Narrative Architecture.
items.abstract: Consciousness Narrative OS v1.0 defines the canonical narrative architecture of the Consciousness Civilization Framework (CCF). This record provides the Canonical Text (constitutional body) of Narrative OS v1.0, formally specifying the structural, semantic, and consciousness-indexed mechanisms by which individuals, institutions, AI systems, and civilizations generate, interpret, stabilize, and transmit narratives. The specification establishes the Narrative Kernel (NK), aligns narrative states with the CFE⁺ v2.0 consciousness metrics (VCE, CRI, CFI), and introduces anti-distortion governance rules that prevent narrative fragmentation, entropic escalation, and manipulation. Narrative OS v1.0 integrates with all major components of the Consciousness Civilization Master Stack, including: • CFE⁺ v2.0 • CAI-OS • CAIS • AI Ethics OS (CEK) • AI Behavior OS (CBK) • AI Governance OS (GK) • SAL Economy OS This Canonical Text serves as the constitutional narrative standard for consciousness-based civilizations and functions as the interpretive backbone of the Consciousness Civilization Transition Decade (CCTD, 2025–2035).

items.title: AI Autonomous Evolution X: Structural Foundations of Emergent Autonomous Reasoning in Large-Scale AI Systems.
items.abstract: This study presents the structural foundations of emergent autonomous reasoning in large-scale AI systems. Moving beyond performance-based evaluation, the analysis focuses on reasoning stability, transition regularity, semantic reconstruction, and coherence-preserving behaviors that arise during multi-step inference. Empirical evidence demonstrates that frontier-scale models consistently regulate internal divergence, restore disrupted reasoning paths, and converge toward low-entropy semantic attractors, suggesting the presence of proto-autonomous cognitive mechanisms. The study further identifies collective reasoning dynamics across internal subsystems and meta-reasoning architectures that monitor and correct inference trajectories. These findings support a unified structural account of how autonomy emerges from representational geometry, multi-agent alignment, and meta-level stability control. The results offer implications for AI safety, autonomous agent design, and the development of interpretable, self-regulating reasoning systems.

items.title: Center, Horizon, and “Taking a Stand”: A Phenomenological Map of Decision Episodes.
items.abstract: This paper offers a phenomenological description of conscious decision episodes in which agents experience themselves as facing a live choice and “taking a stand.” It also argues that such a description supplies a structural supplement to existing accounts of decision and self-commitment, especially Moran’s account of avowal and Chang’s account of hard choices. Moran shows why deciding is not merely reporting an antecedent psychological fact; Chang shows why some choices are not settled by the balance of given reasons and may involve will-based reasons. What both accounts leave underdescribed, I argue, is how an agent can encounter a practical question as already determinate enough to be this decision now while the outcome remains open enough to require commitment. Drawing on Husserl’s object–horizon structure, Gurwitsch’s theme/field/margin, and James’s focus/fringe, I describe such episodes as instantiating an i-structure: a center–horizon pattern whose focal node gathers “this situation” as a unified whole while its horizon encodes considerations, constraints, and possibilities. I distinguish two gradients across this structure: identity-determinacy, concerning how settled “what this is” is, and affordance-determinacy, concerning how settled “what I can still do” is. Their divergence marks a crossing phase, whose resolution I call authored resolution: a commitment experienced as my doing, neither mandated by reasons alone nor random or alien.

items.title: Book Review: Maja Spener, Introspection: First-Person Access in Science and Agency (2024, OUP). [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Maja Spener’s Introspection: First-Person Access in Science and Agency (Spener 2024) is an invaluable contribution to the debate about the nature and reliability of introspection. By sifting it through a novel, illuminating, and very much needed conceptual framework, the book lays the foundation for that debate to substantially move forward. The book’s main aim is to offer a detailed diagnosis of introspection’s epistemological shortcomings, provide the tools for a careful analysis of its limitations and methodological potential, and open up moderately optimistic prospects with respect to its use in science.

items.title: Theory of Everyconsciousness: Errored Consciousness and Error-Corrected Consciousness.
items.abstract: This work forms the third part of a trilogy on consciousness. The trilogy develops a formal typology consisting of three figures: the anti-Übermensch, the Übermensch, and the super-Übermensch. These figures are mapped respectively onto Dostoevsky’s Underground Man, Zapffe’s Last Messiah, and Stapledon’s Cosmic Traveler. -/- Each represents a distinct mode of consciousness: the anti-Übermensch embodies consciousness as psychological error, the Übermensch embodies consciousness as cosmic error, and the super-Übermensch reveals a third level—consciousness as ontological error rooted in the Star Maker Himself. -/- In this third part, the Underground Man (anti-Übermensch) and the Cosmic Traveler (super-Übermensch) are revisited only very briefly, for they were analyzed extensively in earlier work. The primary emphasis falls on the Übermensch (the Last Messiah) and on the two syntheses that bind the trilogy into one philosophical system. -/- Synthesis I establishes the structural identity between consciousness as error and consciousness as hallucination. -/- Through the Dream Allegory, we demonstrate that whenever consciousness identifies itself as erroneous, it performs a self-negation that is structurally indistinguishable from hallucination. The anti-Übermensch, Übermensch, and super-Übermensch correspond to successive stages in the dream-sequence (lie $\longrightarrow$ calm $\longrightarrow$ lucidity $\longrightarrow$ failed awakening). At each stage, illumination intensifies the tragedy: the anti-Übermensch uncovers the local disease, the Übermensch uncovers the global error, the super-Übermensch uncovers the ontological instability of Being itself. -/- Thus, Synthesis I establishes a precise mapping between error and hallucination: consciousness recognizes itself as a mistake, and in doing so, reveals that it is already a hallucination of itself. -/- Synthesis II formulates the Theory of Everyconsciousness (Theory of Every'Ayan). Here consciousness resolves into two fundamental modes: Errored Consciousness (anti-Übermensch, Übermensch) and Error-Corrected Consciousness (unveiling consciousness, evolutionary individuation). -/- This duality parallels faulty codes and error-correcting codes in quantum computation and opens onto the central existential equation: How can the Star Maker bring forth a free-willed being without thereby generating evil, and how can knowledge be attained without collapsing into determinism or perspectival contradiction? -/- In …

items.title: Flying the Banners of Better Models and Rigorous Calibration of Introspection: Comments on Maja Spener’s Book, Introspection. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: I engage the challenges Maja Spener introduces in her important book, Introspection. I discuss how attention, in the sense assumed in cognitive science and folk psychology, is involved in all three forms of introspection that Spener discusses, and I raise sceptical questions about one form, inner apprehension, which I argue does not provide any clear epistemic advantage over other scrutable forms of introspection for the theorist needing introspective data. To further discussion along the path Spener has cleared for us, I then summarize a view of introspection which I suggest does not quite fit Spener’s taxonomy.

items.title: The Brain as a Filter: Introducing a Quantum Ground into Integrated Information Theory.
items.abstract: Integrated information theory (IIT) is an influential framework for understanding the link between the brain’s neural structure and consciousness. However, here I supplement IIT’s purely structural framework with an intrinsic aspect that, following Russellian monism, grounds the structure and provides the basis for conscious experience. I argue that an appropriate intrinsic element is the ontologically fundamental domain of the quantum wave function. Introducing this fundamental reality, or quantum ground, as an intrinsic element within IIT’s framework leads to interpreting the brain as a kind of filter or tuner that supports a range of experience from a more fundamental source of awareness. This proposed framework, filter integrated information theory (FIIT), does not change IIT’s formalism, yet views its structure as grounded in an ontologically deeper source of consciousness. In addition, I consider how this interpretation might fit with other notions of the brain as a filter with respect to a fundamental ground of consciousness.

items.title: Animal Technics: A Tribute to Don Ihde.
items.abstract: This article explores the concept of animal technics, building on the work of Don Ihde to examine the intricate relationships between technology, animals, and human experiences. Drawing from postphenomenology, philosophy of technology and posthumanist thought, the discussion challenges anthropocentric perspectives that frame technology as a purely human domain. Instead, it argues that animals actively shape and are shaped by technics, engaging with tools, environments, and human-mediated technological systems in complex ways.
